    Projection to RR kills every positive-weight transition, and a telescope with zero transitions is zero. Projection to HH retains the ghost-free word (6.10). The resulting system consists of injective Verma maps and has a nonzero filtered colimit; the affine realization has the same property.

    Moreover, for I=ker⁡(B→R)I=\ker(B\to R), every finite map

    I⊗B𝐋N⟶BI^{\otimes_B^{\mathbf L}N}\longrightarrow B

    induced by the ideal inclusion is nonzero. Thus both the tensor-object and fibre-map descent routes through B→RB\to R fail at this parameter. The proof is A nonzero native telescope killed by the zero-weight augmentation, §§2–4.

    The unit on the telescope itself can be determined. There is an all-level sufficient condition under the smooth realization (6.1). Suppose a native complex has a strict dg BB-module representative XX with Xq=0X^q=0 below a fixed cochain degree. On positive currents the model (6.2) for ΦX\Phi X has terms C𝔤⊗XqC_{\mathfrak g}\otimes X^q, which are injective in the smooth positive-current category. This bounded-below complex is K-injective there. Its positive-current invariants are δ1⊗X\delta_1\otimes X. Every LxiL_{x_i} kills δ1\delta_1, so its differential on these invariants is dXd_X. A smooth affine K-injective replacement restricts to a positive-current K-injective resolution, and evaluation of the tensor–Hom unit on the inducing vector is the inclusion of these very invariants. This proves that ηX\eta_X is invertible. The hypothesis bounds the actual cochain representative. Internal energies can be arbitrarily negative.

    Each FjF_j above has nonnegative cochain terms, so the cone of 1−shift1-\mathrm{shift} representing LL has no terms below degree −1-1. Thus the same LL satisfies (6.11) and L→∼ΨΦLL\xrightarrow{\sim}\Psi\Phi L. It is detected by realization even though zero-weight base change kills it. More generally, in every simple type and at every s=a/b≤0s=a/b\le0 rational, choose u+a<0u+a<0 in the alternating-root construction. All pairings u+(2j−1)au+(2j-1)a now stay negative. The embeddings point from the old Verma into the new one, with successively lower top energies. Inducing their horizontal top maps gives a telescope of nonnegative native complexes. Zero-weight base change kills all the transitions. Ghost base change retains their injective even-current maps, hence gives a nonzero union. The cochain bound again proves that this telescope has invertible unit. For positive rational ss, the finite staircase above allows the initial weight to depend on NN.

    The fibre J=ker⁡(B→H)J=\ker(B\to H) retains a different obstruction. At 𝔰𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_2 raw level −3-3, let cc be the weight-one ghost dual to ftft, where [e,f]=h[e,f]=h. On a horizontal Verma top vλv_\lambda, the differential between the unique weight-(λ+2)(\lambda+2) vectors e−1vλe_{-1}v_\lambda and c⊗vλc\otimes v_\lambda has coefficient, up to the common cochain sign,

    f1e−1vλ=(−3−λ)vλ.f_1e_{-1}v_\lambda=(-3-\lambda)v_\lambda .

    At λ=−3\lambda=-3 this is zero. Thus cc survives in H1(B)1H^1(B)_1 and the first map J→BJ\to B is nonzero. For every simple type at every level, the highest long root gives the same test by taking λ(hθ)\lambda(h_\theta) equal to the raw scalar level. Nevertheless any strict representative annihilated by a fixed JdJ^d has good unit under (6.1), because the quotients of its finite ghost filtration are inflated from HH. In B/J2B/J^2 the first ghost still acts nontrivially on cohomology, giving a concrete example beyond the inflated objects. At raw −3-3 the unit also holds on B⊗R𝐋TB\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}T for arbitrary unbounded horizontal TT, by A finite cofree resolution for arbitrary horizontal coefficients at raw level minus three. Invertibility for every ordinary BB-complex at this level remains open. At the parameters with a realization kernel, the full kernel, its localization and the essential image on the quotient also remain to be determined.

    6.9 Cellularity and derived torsion

    There is another plausible description of the image in (6.8), expressed directly in positive-current modules. To keep its ideal distinct from I⊂YkI\subset Y_k, put

    U+=U(t𝔤[t]),𝔞=ker⁡(U+→ℂ).U_+=U(t\mathfrak g[t]),\qquad \mathfrak a=\ker(U_+\to\mathbb C).

    A smooth module is jointly augmentation-torsion if every vector vv is killed by one whole power 𝔞r\mathfrak a^r. The exponent may depend on vv, but it must work for every element of that ideal power. Let 𝒯⊂Sm⁡(Aℓ)\mathcal T\subset\operatorname{Sm}(A_\ell) be this torsion category and set

    D𝔞={M∈𝒮ℓ:Hq(M)∈𝒯 for every q}.D_{\mathfrak a}= \{M\in\mathscr S_\ell:H^q(M)\in\mathcal T \text{ for every }q\}.

    The cellular category 𝒞\mathscr C generated by WW and its required shifts lies in D𝔞D_{\mathfrak a}.

    Finite augmentation quotients explain a substantial converse. Since 𝔤\mathfrak g is simple, U+U_+ is generated in positive current degree one, and

    𝔞r=⨁d≥r(U+)d.\mathfrak a^r=\bigoplus_{d\ge r}(U_+)_d.

    The quotient U+/𝔞rU_+/\mathfrak a^r is finite dimensional. The induced module

    Er=Aℓ⊗U+(U+/𝔞r)E_r=A_\ell\otimes_{U_+}(U_+/\mathfrak a^r)

    has a finite filtration with factors

    W⟨−j⟩⊗ℂ(U+)j,0≤j<r,W\langle-j\rangle\otimes_{\mathbb C}(U_+)_j, \qquad 0\le j<r,

    where the last factor is a multiplicity space. Resolutions by such modules show that every complex whose terms are torsion is cellular. Every object with bounded-below torsion cohomology is also cellular. These statements, and the cellular coreflector on the whole unbounded smooth category, are proved in Augmentation torsion and unbounded affine cellularization.

    The torsion inclusion has its own derived adjunction,

    i:D(𝒯)⇄D(Sm⁡(Aℓ)):RΓ𝔞.i:D(\mathcal T)\rightleftarrows D(\operatorname{Sm}(A_\ell)):R\Gamma_{\mathfrak a}.
    (6.12)

    It differs from both (6.1) and the inclusion of 𝒞\mathscr C. In particular, the exact inclusion of abelian categories need not induce a fully faithful functor on their unbounded derived categories.

    This failure occurs already for positive-current 𝔰𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_2, before adjoining negative affine modes. Let 𝒮+=Sm⁡(t𝔰𝔩2[t])\mathcal S_+=\operatorname{Sm}(t\mathfrak{sl}_2[t]), let 𝒯+\mathcal T_+ be its joint-torsion subcategory, and put

    en=n(n+1)2,X=⨁n≥1ℂ[n]⟨−en⟩.e_n=\frac{n(n+1)}2,\qquad X=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb C[n]\langle-e_n\rangle.

    For the actual derived torsion adjunction one has

    H0RΓ𝔞(iX)0≅∏n≥1Kn⨁n≥1Kn≠0,dim⁡Kn=2n+1.H^0R\Gamma_{\mathfrak a}(iX)_0 \cong \frac{\prod_{n\ge1}K_n}{\bigoplus_{n\ge1}K_n}\ne0, \qquad \dim K_n=2n+1.
    (6.13)

    But H0X=0H^0X=0. Hence the unit of this torsion adjunction is not invertible. Its counit on the cellular object iXiX also fails to be an equivalence, so it cannot be the cellular coreflection there. Without an energy grading the corresponding quotient still injects into degree-zero cohomology. An explicit positive-current splitting transfers the failure to affine raw level zero; no transfer to arbitrary affine level is asserted. See An unbounded joint-torsion unit failure for positive-current sl2.

    Finite quotients nevertheless admit a precise local-duality theorem. For an integer N≥1N\ge1, put

    𝔫=t𝔰𝔩2[t],𝔤N=𝔫/tN𝔰𝔩2[t],RN=U(𝔤N),dN=3(N−1).\mathfrak n=t\mathfrak{sl}_2[t],\quad \mathfrak g_N=\mathfrak n/t^N\mathfrak{sl}_2[t],\quad R_N=U(\mathfrak g_N),\quad d_N=3(N-1).

    Let JNJ_N be the augmentation ideal of RNR_N and ENcof=lim→r⁡(RN/JNr)∨E_N^{\mathrm{cof}}=\varinjlim_r(R_N/J_N^r)^\vee, with action (bϕ)(a)=ϕ(ab)(b\phi)(a)=\phi(ab). In the actual positive-current smooth category,

    RΓ𝔞(RN)≃ENcof⊗(det⁡𝔤N)∨[−dN].R\Gamma_{\mathfrak a}(R_N) \simeq E_N^{\mathrm{cof}}\otimes (\det\mathfrak g_N)^\vee[-d_N].
    (6.14)

    The comparison identifies the actual torsion counit. In the graded convention the determinant-dual line has energy 3N(N−1)/23N(N-1)/2. The proof first uses finite-dimensional Lie-algebra duality, then compares the inflated counit cone through finite Chevalley complexes with bounded coefficient terms. It proves (6.14) for these objects, not a formula on arbitrary unbounded coefficients. See Actual torsion of the smooth regular quotients and its finite-quotient local-duality argument.

    The full unbounded equality 𝒞=D𝔞\mathscr C=D_{\mathfrak a} remains a separate question. Non-full-faithfulness of (6.12) does not decide that equality of object classes. Nor does termwise vanishing of a torsion functor prove vanishing of its derived value: a concrete quotient complex in the graded positive-current category has zero torsion in every term but is cellular and has nonzero actual derived torsion. K-injective replacement changes the calculation. This example is computed in The graded quotient does not give an outside or kernel object.

    A common current tail gives actual completeness

    Smooth-vector completeness is a different comparison from affine induction and from derived augmentation torsion. Put

    𝔫=t𝔰𝔩2[t],𝔫L=tL𝔰𝔩2[t],F:D(𝒮)⟶D(𝔐),G=Rsm⁡,\mathfrak n=t\mathfrak{sl}_2[t],\qquad \mathfrak n_L=t^L\mathfrak{sl}_2[t],\qquad F:D(\mathcal S)\longrightarrow D(\mathfrak M), \quad G=R\operatorname{sm},

    where 𝒮\mathcal S is the smooth positive-current module category and 𝔐\mathfrak M is the category of all positive-current modules. Use algebraic integer-energy gradings, with currents lowering energy and maps preserving it. Products are taken energy by energy before the outer algebraic direct sum.

    Suppose one tail annihilates all sufficiently low cohomology: there are L≥1L\ge1 and an integer bb such that

    𝔫LHq(X)=0(q≤b).\mathfrak n_LH^q(X)=0\qquad(q\le b).

    Then the actual unit is an equivalence,

    X→∼GF(X)≃holimn⁡τ≥−nX,X\xrightarrow{\sim}GF(X) \simeq\operatorname{holim}_n\tau^{\ge-n}X,

    with no bound on higher cohomology, multiplicities or energy support. For every smooth derived source YY, the original map

    HomD(𝒮)⁡(Y,X)⟶HomD(𝔐)⁡(FY,FX)\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal S)}(Y,X) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathfrak M)}(FY,FX)

    is an isomorphism, including all shifts. Common-tail completeness.

    The proof first restricts to a tail on which the cohomology layers are genuinely trivial. A sufficiently deeper restriction splits the Postnikov extensions coherently enough to identify the original completion map. If the same annihilating tail works in every degree, the whole restricted complex becomes noncanonically formal; M=4L−2M=4L-2 is a sufficient deeper-tail index. With the hypothesis only for q≤bq\le b, this formality statement applies to the lower truncation. No formality over the original positive-current algebra is asserted.

    Completeness does not settle generation by the shifted trivial modules. Writing

    ℒ=Loc⁡{ℂ⟨e⟩:e∈ℤ},\mathcal L=\operatorname{Loc}\{\mathbb C\langle e\rangle:e\in\mathbb Z\},

    the equality of ℒ\mathcal L with the full subcategory of joint augmentation-torsion cohomology remains open. A potential nonzero torsion-cohomology object in ℒ⟂\mathcal L^\perp may be complete and may have a common annihilating tail; its current action must be nontrivial in arbitrarily low cohomological degrees. The smooth derived category is itself not left-complete. The common-tail theorem locates a large complete class within it, rather than identifying completeness with cellularity. The separate generation question.

    Energy bounds for the smooth unit and the torsion counit

    Another criterion reaches both comparisons. Continue with positive-current 𝔰𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_2, algebraic integer-energy gradings and smooth XX. Suppose HqXH^qX vanishes below energy bqb_q, taking bq=+∞b_q=+\infty for a zero group. Write ep=p(p+1)/2e_p=p(p+1)/2 as in (6.13). If, for each fixed integer tt,

    bt−p+ep⟶+∞(p→∞),b_{t-p}+e_p\longrightarrow+\infty\qquad(p\to\infty),

    then X→GFXX\to GFX and iRΓ𝔞X→XiR\Gamma_{\mathfrak a}X\to X are equivalences, and XX belongs to the localizing subcategory generated by the energy-shifted trivial modules. There is no common-tail hypothesis here.

    The estimate comes from the minimal resolution for the tail tN𝔰𝔩2[t]t^N\mathfrak{sl}_2[t]. At homological degree pp its generators lower energy by at least Np+(p2)≥epNp+\binom p2\ge e_p. For a cohomology layer with floor bqb_q, a degree-preserving map from the resolution shifted to energy ee can contribute to Extp⁡\operatorname{Ext}^p only if e≥bq+epe\ge b_q+e_p. This bound also applies to finite augmentation quotients by filtering them by shifted trivial modules. Thus for fixed output degree and energy the tests for both functors stabilize at a single finite truncation, uniformly in the tail and the quotient. The smooth unit follows first from the ambient module truncations. Its identification then permits the same finite calculation for the torsion counit.

    For instance bq≥−cq2−C|q|−D0b_q\ge-cq^2-C|q|-D_0 in sufficiently negative degrees suffices if 0≤c<1/20\le c<1/2. At the quadratic boundary in (6.13) the layers instead have b−p=−epb_{-p}=-e_p. Infinitely many align in energy zero, and the quotient of a product by a direct sum displayed there measures the failure of the torsion comparison. The object in that example is still cellular. The unrestricted question about generation by the shifted trivial modules therefore survives this calculation.

    For ordinary affine induction the nonrational result identifies the exact subcategory generated by the regular horizontal top in every simple type. Passing from that algebraic category to a physical boundary theory would require independently defined line objects and their collision products. To ask how a bulk operation acts on them one must also require compatibility with maps between lines. That requirement leads to actions and derived centres.

    Part II Duality and centresChapter 7 of 18

    7

    Actions and derived centres

    A boundary observer may detect a bulk insertion even when its value on the vacuum vanishes. In a free field theory on a half-space, a bulk field whose linear projection is zero acts on a boundary current by the scalar ℏκ\hbar\kappa. The calculation uses the positions of the insertions and the contraction of the eliminated field. It suggests asking which families of operations a boundary algebra can detect and which are determined by evaluation on a distinguished state.

    Two comparison problems arise. One computes derived maps from a small exterior algebra into a vertex algebra. The other asks whether an operation on a factorizing coalgebra is determined by its value on the vacuum. Both lead to explicit rational differential forms and residues. Their conclusions concern different mapping spaces, so the map connecting those spaces must itself be constructed.

    7.1 Central operations on modules

    Let AA be a unital associative algebra over a characteristic-zero field kk. Its centre is

    Z(A)={z∈A:za=az for every a∈A}.Z(A)=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for every }a\in A\}.

    For every left AA-module MM, a central element gives an AA-linear operator m↦zmm\mapsto zm, naturally in MM. Conversely, every natural endomorphism of the identity functor on AA-modules arises this way. Indeed, its value on the regular module is determined by z=ηA(1)z=\eta_A(1). Naturality with respect to right multiplication by aa gives az=zaaz=za; naturality with respect to A→M,b↦bmA\to M, b\mapsto bm, then gives ηM(m)=zm\eta_M(m)=zm.

    Thus the same element acts compatibly on every representation. This explains why a centre is relevant to bulk–boundary questions: an operation that can be moved without changing its interaction with boundary observables should produce compatible operators on boundary representations. Additional geometric structure is needed to turn this motivation into a statement about a field theory.

    The module interpretation also explains the derived replacement. Write Ae=A⊗kAopA^e=A\otimes_k A^{\mathrm{op}}. An AA-bimodule map A→AA\to A is determined by a central element, so

    Z(A)=HomAe⁡(A,A).Z(A)=\operatorname{Hom}_{A^e}(A,A).

    Replacing Hom by its derived functor gives the Hochschild cochain complex

    C∙(A,A)≃RHomAe⁡(A,A).C^\bullet(A,A)\simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_{A^e}(A,A).

    For an ordinary algebra over kk, the bar resolution represents this complex by Cn(A,A)=Homk⁡(A⊗n,A)C^n(A,A)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^{\otimes n},A). Its first differentials are

    (bz)(a)=az−za,(bf)(a1,a2)=a1f(a2)−f(a1a2)+f(a1)a2.(bz)(a)=az-za,\qquad (bf)(a_1,a_2)=a_1f(a_2)-f(a_1a_2)+f(a_1)a_2.

    Consequently HH0(A)=Z(A)HH^0(A)=Z(A), while HH1(A)HH^1(A) consists of derivations modulo inner derivations. Higher degrees retain further compatibility data.

    A class represented by a bimodule map A→A[n]A\to A[n] acts on a derived left module through

    M≃A⊗ALM⟶A[n]⊗ALM≃M[n].M\simeq A\otimes_A^L M \longrightarrow A[n]\otimes_A^L M\simeq M[n].

    Here differentials have degree +1+1, and V[1]j=Vj+1V[1]^j=V^{j+1}. The derived centre retains these operations and their coherent compositions. Hochschild cochains carry an E2E_2-algebra structure: products are accompanied by homotopies encoding their interchange. On cohomology this includes the cup product and the degree-minus-one Gerstenhaber bracket. An equivalence of underlying complexes alone does not identify those operations. See Higher Algebra, §5.3.1 and Gerstenhaber’s construction.

    For a small calculation, take A=k[x]/(x2)A=k[x]/(x^2). The ordinary centre is all of AA. A derivation is determined by f(x)=a+bxf(x)=a+bx, but

    0=f(x2)=2xf(x)=2ax0=f(x^2)=2x f(x)=2ax

    forces a=0a=0. Since AA is commutative, inner derivations vanish. Hence

    HH0(A)=k⊕︎kx,HH1(A)=kδ,δ(x)=x.HH^0(A)=k\oplus kx,\qquad HH^1(A)=k\delta, \qquad \delta(x)=x.

    The higher operation is visible even here: [δ,x]=δ(x)=x[\delta,x]=\delta(x)=x. The centre and the degree-one class do not merely coexist as vector spaces; the bracket records how the derivation acts on the central element. A list of cohomology dimensions would omit this information.

    7.2 A bulk insertion acting on a boundary current

    Take the abelian half-space theory with response operator κ∂z\kappa\partial_z, normal coordinate t≥0t\geq0 and boundary coordinate zz. Work with regular observables whose smooth test kernels have compact support at each finite field number. Over an open set VV in the boundary, choose a smooth profile of integral one supported in 0≤t<ε0\leq t<\varepsilon. It gives a cochain inclusion iqi^q of the boundary current complex 𝒜κ(V)\mathcal A_\kappa(V) into the collar observables. Integration in the normal direction gives the linear projection pp. Its quantum extension also counts pair contractions involving the fields being integrated out,

    7.3 A factorizing actor and its pointing

    Work on X=𝔸k1X=\mathbb A^1_k. A differential module is a sheaf with an action of differential operators; it keeps track of how coefficients vary with position. We use coaugmented, counital coalgebras with empty coefficient kk. A factorizing coalgebra assigns complexes of differential modules to finite labelled configurations, including their ordered collision charts. For an ordered division I=A⊔BI=A\sqcup B, its coproduct restricts on the locus where the two blocks are disjoint to an equivalence

    FI|UA,B≃(FA⊠FB)|UA,B.F_I\big|_{U_{A,B}} \simeq (F_A\boxtimes F_B)\big|_{U_{A,B}}.

    Successive divisions come with coassociativity homotopies and their higher compatibilities. Maps preserve these data, including the collision restrictions. The two orders A|BA|B and B|AB|A are distinct data unless a suitable cocommutative structure is supplied.

    We call such a coalgebra an actor when it parametrizes operations on another object. The word does not add a multiplication to FF. Two tensor products occur. Disjoint convolution, written ⋆\star, combines configurations by splitting their labels; its unit KK is concentrated at the empty configuration. The tensor ⊗!\otimes^! combines two coefficient systems at the same configuration by extraordinary pullback along the diagonal. Its unit JJ has the local unit coefficient at each configuration. A pointing is an actual coherent coalgebra map

    u:J⟶F.u:J\longrightarrow F.

    It specifies a vacuum operation together with all its compatibility homotopies. It contains more information than a class in the singleton cohomology. These conventions are those of the ordered-collision coalgebra construction, particularly its coalgebra category and diagonal tensor.

    The smallest useful test algebra has two orthogonal idempotents:

    B=kp1⊕︎kp2,pipj=δijpi.B=kp_1\oplus kp_2,\qquad p_ip_j=\delta_{ij}p_i.

    Let C=CBC=C_B be its Chevalley coalgebra: its coefficients are built from finite partitions with a BB-label on each block, and its differential merges blocks using the product of BB. It has multiplication m:C⊗!C→Cm:C\otimes^!C\to C and total unit pointing uB:J→Cu_B:J\to C. The two idempotents distinguish two colours of input and output.

    A character of (F,u)(F,u) is a coalgebra map g:F→Cg:F\to C together with a specified homotopy gu≃uBgu\simeq u_B. An action is a coalgebra map α:F⊗!C→C\alpha:F\otimes^!C\to C together with a specified homotopy α(u⊗!1C)≃1C\alpha(u\otimes^!1_C)\simeq1_C. There is no additional associative-action axiom involving a multiplication on FF. To retain the specified homotopies and homotopies between them, define the complete spaces

    𝒳(F,u)=hofibuB⁡[MapCoalg⁡(F,C)→u∗MapCoalg⁡(J,C)],𝒜C(F,u)=hofib1C⁡[MapCoalg⁡(F⊗!C,C)→(u⊗!1C)∗MapCoalg⁡(C,C)].\begin{aligned} \mathcal X(F,u) &=\operatorname{hofib}_{u_B}\left[ \operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(F,C) \xrightarrow{u^*}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(J,C)\right],\\ \mathcal A_C(F,u) &=\operatorname{hofib}_{1_C}\left[ \operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(F\otimes^!C,C) \xrightarrow{(u\otimes^!1_C)^*}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(C,C)\right]. \end{aligned}

    A homotopy fibre records a point upstairs and a path from its image to the specified base point; its higher simplices record the remaining compatibilities.

    There are explicit maps

    Θ(g)=m(g⊗!1C),Ψ(α)=α(1F⊗!uB).\Theta(g)=m(g\otimes^!1_C),\qquad \Psi(\alpha)=\alpha(1_F\otimes^!u_B).

    The first turns a character into an operation by multiplication. The second evaluates an operation on the target vacuum. The unit identity gives ΨΘ≃1\Psi\Theta\simeq1. Recognition asks whether ΘΨ≃1\Theta\Psi\simeq1 as well, on the full action space. This requires a coherent reconstruction of the operation, not only agreement on singleton values.

    A centre representing this geometric action problem would be a pointed actor ZCZ_C with a universal action, such that

    naturally for every admitted actor. Existence is part of that assertion. It does not identify the action problem with the Hochschild complex of the two-dimensional algebra BB.

    7.4 Recognition on Chevalley coalgebras

    Let VV be a dg chiral algebra. Its main-diagonal Chevalley coalgebra CVC_V is built from finite partitions of the labelled inputs, with a VV-coefficient on each block. Its differential combines the internal differential of VV with mergers using the chiral product. “Main-diagonal” specifies where the original one-point coefficients enter this construction; it is not a replacement by the cohomology of VV.

    Recognition theorem. Suppose VV is any unbounded dg chiral algebra over a characteristic-zero field on 𝔸1\mathbb A^1, with a genuine closed horizontal unit. For every coherent coassociative pointing u:J→CVu:J\to C_V, the maps Θ\Theta and Ψ\Psi are inverse equivalences between 𝒳(CV,u)\mathcal X(C_V,u) and 𝒜C(CV,u)\mathcal A_C(C_V,u). No homotopy from uu to the genuine unit pointing is required. The equivalence is natural under all pointed coalgebra maps between these objects, including those that preserve no chosen presentation. Arbitrary-pointing recognition.

    The proof resolves the complete mapping diagrams and filters the terms by mismatches between input and output colours. The genuine unit supplies a contraction of the absolute layers. The arbitrary pointing determines the restriction map between those layers; it is retained throughout. Taking the fibre of that restriction gives the relative layer, whose contraction includes the correction joining the two absolute contractions. At each fixed configuration only finitely many partition steps occur. This finite geometric filtration proves an equivalence of the nonlinear mapping spaces even when the coefficient complexes are unbounded. Vanishing of a tangent complex at one point would not establish the same assertion.

    There is also a module family. For an arbitrary unbounded complex MM of right differential modules, form P(M)P(M) by assigning either a unit coefficient or an MM-coefficient to each label. In a summand with several MM-labels, those labels must occupy distinct positions, and an MM-label is last in any equality block containing it. Restrict the external tensor of the assigned coefficients to that open, extend it by the direct-image functor, and sum over assignments. Projection to the summand with only unit coefficients gives P(M)→JP(M)\to J.

    For

    F=P(M)⊗!CV,h:F⟶CV,F=P(M)\otimes^!C_V,\qquad h:F\longrightarrow C_V,

Recognition therefore holds for every uu in this family. No boundedness, finite generation, holonomicity or restriction on the connection of MM is imposed. The proof contracts the positive MM-sectors as two-sided coefficient modules, rather than requiring the pointing to preserve those sectors. Radical reduction.

    A nonunital chiral algebra WW has a genuine unitization W+=W⊕︎ωXW^+=W\oplus\omega_X, where ωX\omega_X is the right differential-module unit on the curve. The inclusion gives i:CW→CW+i:C_W\to C_{W^+}, pointed upstairs by the entire composite iuiu.

    The two requirements measure different possible defects. Based loops test extra automorphisms in the component of the trivial action, but they cannot detect another component of the whole zero sector. Nor can endomorphism composition be replaced by loop addition: composition multiplies the detected scalars and has identity scalar 11, while loop concatenation adds scalars and has identity 00. The proved splitting is a statement about spaces over the scalar set, with no product decomposition for composition. The remaining equivalence.

    7.6 Residues with spectators

    Adding fixed field insertions to the source produces rational forms with spectators: labelled positions z1,…,zrz_1,\ldots,z_r that remain as parameters while auxiliary marked positions w1,…,wmw_1,\ldots,w_m are differentiated or absorbed by residues. Three sets of nonnegative integer bounds control the poles: NijN_{ij} for spectator pairs, bjb_j for a marked point meeting spectator jj, and a positive odd integer μ\mu for marked pairs.

    Denote the resulting complex by Dr,q(b,N;μ)D_{r,q}(b,N;\mu). A residue lowers form degree by one and increases ss by one, so both differential terms raise 2s+i2s+i by one.     The charge-one case explains why the charge restriction in the theorem below matters. With one spectator and N=0N=0, put y=w−zy=w-z. The complex is

    Strict three-spectator theorem. For r=3r=3, every bj,Nij≥0b_j,N_{ij}\ge0, every positive odd μ\mu, and every charge q≥2q\ge2,

This is a chain isomorphism between those modules, not an assertion that the factor is a unit in the polynomial base.

    7.7 The remaining comparison

    The geometric action problem also has concrete higher homotopies. For arbitrary unbounded coassociative actors, the prescribed three-block pointed boundary has a filling with its original root, marks and scalar pointing retained. Its construction uses two genuine vacuum labels, their proper deletion edges and full differential-module residue maps; it cancels the action-generated residue without declaring the entire normal kernel contractible. No cocommutativity assumption is needed. Three-block filling.

    A separate comparison of two prescribed mixed primitives holds on the old separated locus z0≠z1z_0\ne z_1 when the underlying FF has a supplied coherent cocommutative structure. The action and pointing themselves need only be coassociative. It fills the specified closed difference and its corner restriction; it does not extend across the old collision diagonal. These hypotheses must remain distinct from those of the three-block theorem. Separated-base primitive comparison.

    Recognition for arbitrary pointed factorizing actors still asks for Θ\Theta to be an equivalence with all changes of roots, collision restrictions and arbitrarily long refined words. The three-block filling and the separated primitive comparison provide particular coherences. For each finite exterior algebra on degree-one generators the ordinary vertex mapping space is known. Comparing it with an action on an independent boundary must additionally preserve the original actor, both roof legs, evaluation and every required incoming refinement. Even a cofinal system of suitable state resolutions of the Heisenberg tensor source would suffice for the roof comparison above. Its existence is open.

    The choice of boundary changes the existence question itself. Replace the two-idempotent boundary CC by the Chevalley coalgebra of the Heisenberg state space k[x1,x2,…]k[x_1,x_2,\ldots] at κ≠0\kappa\ne0. Here J−nJ_{-n} multiplies by xnx_n and JnJ_n acts by κn∂xn\kappa n\partial_{x_n}, for n>0n>0. For the full category of pointed factorizing actions on this coalgebra, there are two parallel maps of actions which remain in distinct components after every map out of their target. They are built from exterior actors on two and one generators and the action associated to ∂x1\partial_{x_1}. The distinction survives because the vacuum forces every degree-zero one-root operation of a receiving action to be a module map, while the nonzero derivation ∂x1\partial_{x_1} cannot be such a map. A representing action would be terminal, so its mapping spaces would supply a path equalizing the two composites. This proves nonrepresentability for this boundary and this action functor.

    To draw the corresponding conclusion about a physical boundary, one needs to realize both maps and their actions by supported physical systems. In the other direction, suppose a physical system is universal among a specified class of bulk–boundary systems. A sufficient condition for its algebraic action to be terminal is that the supported realization induce equivalences on the full mapping spaces and that its image generate the algebraic action category by small colimits. Maps from such a colimit into the image of the universal system form a limit of contractible mapping spaces. The support and collision hypotheses belong to the realization functor itself.

    A marked action at finite quantum precision

    There is another way for evaluation on a vacuum to lose an operation. In the four-current complex for 𝔤𝔩2\mathfrak{gl}_2, take the current colours H,E,F,IH,E,F,I, where II is the trace, and work modulo ℏ3\hbar^3 over R3=ℂ[ℏ]/(ℏ3)R_3=\mathbb C[\hbar]/(\hbar^3). Besides the current states, the complex has odd ghost states. Multiplying the output of a normalized closed field by a closed trace ghost produces a degree-one class. Its scalar vacuum coefficient vanishes, but the constant term of its full value on the two vacua recovers the trace ghost itself. Acting on that same output and pairing against a dual ghost coefficient are different operations. In the pairing, a trace creator on the field acts by contraction on the dual coefficient.

    Keep the ghost output as well as the current state until the last pairing. Let uu denote the separation between an inserted state xx and a fixed, or rooted, current input ww. A retained kernel assigns to x,wx,w a Laurent series in uu valued in current states and in each finite-cutoff quotient of the ghost module. On one right slice a marked coefficient is represented, for the inserted input in question, by

    y=∑i=1m(∑j≥νujFij)⊗bi.y=\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\sum_{j\geq\nu}u^jF_{ij}\right)\otimes b_i .

    The bib_i are a finite list of right current coefficients. Every FijF_{ij} uses the same middle ghost cutoff and takes values in left current coefficients. The order matters. First act on ww by bib_i, then apply the kernel at xx, then contract the middle ghost and act on the output by FijF_{ij}. With the one lower bound ν\nu, the one cutoff and the one right support for the whole series on this slice, the coefficient of a fixed output power is a finite sum. Choosing new cutoffs independently at every jj would lose this argument.

    At noncritical level K≠−2K\ne-2 the coefficient-defined rooted kernel Φ\Phi and the reversed retained field 𝒴♯\mathcal Y^\sharp are chain homotopic in every rooted degree. The homotopy has zero scalar pairing and commutes with the two translations. On the marked source, contracting each trace-ghost entry extends the homotopy to the trace summand. On the positive traceless inserted summand the comparison uses the prescribed state operation 𝒥\mathcal J and the correction Ξ\Xi obtained by differentiating a source homotopy. With these same operations in both evaluations, the homotopy holds on the whole Laurent domain just specified. Chapter 17 gives the primitive and its scalar normalization. Retained kernels.

    An independent physical comparison would have to compute 𝒥+Ξ\mathcal J+\Xi from the two ordered junction products. For example, insert an EE-ghost at one endpoint and an FF-ghost at the other. Both orders must give the prescribed maps, after their separately defined identifications of tensor factors, including the contact where insertions 11 and 33 meet with 22 separated and the unit on each occupied slot. Identifying a physical adjunction further requires its unit, counit and triangle identities in specified module categories. At K=−2K=-2 the retained field and its rooted exchange homotopy exist. The critical algebraic state complex admits a separate translation-compatible linear model with additional generators, including the critical quadratic current. Its marked operations still require comparison on these generators. The critical comparison, the independent physical products and the extension beyond R3R_3 are distinct open questions.

    These questions force attention to the spaces on which operations can be composed. A residue map defined on algebraic rational forms, a homotopy on a separated configuration and an operation on a completed space of fields have different domains. Passing between them requires the specified tensor, support and completion maps. Those maps are the subject of the next chapter.

    Part III Operations and their domainsChapter 8 of 18

    8

    Tensor products, support and completion

    An operation on every finite collection of states need not act on an infinite state. The difficulty can occur before any integral diverges: the proposed output may simply lie outside the vector space on which the next operation is defined. For boundary reconstruction this matters twice. Several incoming representations must first be combined, and the resulting object must then be compared with a space of current operations. These constructions involve different infinite sums. Their order determines the comparison map.

    8.1 Tensor completion and matrix rank

    Consider the vector space V=ℂℕV=\mathbb C^{\mathbb N} of all complex sequences. The natural map

    V⊗ℂV⟶ℂℕ×ℕ,f⊗g⟼(figj)i,j≥0,V\otimes_{\mathbb C}V\longrightarrow \mathbb C^{\mathbb N\times\mathbb N}, \qquad f\otimes g\longmapsto(f_i g_j)_{i,j\geq0},

    has image the matrices of finite rank. A sum of rr elementary tensors has column space contained in the span of rr sequences; conversely, a finite-rank matrix can be expressed using a basis of its column space. The infinite identity matrix (δij)(\delta_{ij}) therefore does not belong to this image.

    Give the image the coordinatewise topology inherited from the full matrix space. Its completion is the full matrix space: finite-support matrices are dense, and the finite diagonal matrices converge coordinatewise to (δij)(\delta_{ij}). The identity matrix becomes available after this specified completion. Nothing in this calculation identifies the completion with a tensor product defined using a different topology.

    The same issue appears in the current constructions below, where matrix indices are replaced by cohomological degrees, bar lengths, current modes and Laurent exponents. We will keep these indices separate long enough to see which infinite expressions the operations can act on.

    8.2 Algebraic tensors and mapping complexes

    For cochain complexes M,NM,N, with differential of degree +1+1, the algebraic tensor complex has

    (M⊗N)n=⨁i+j=nMi⊗Nj,d(m⊗n)=dm⊗n+(−1)|m|m⊗dn.(M\otimes N)^n=\bigoplus_{i+j=n}M^i\otimes N^j, \qquad d(m\otimes n)=dm\otimes n+(-1)^{|m|}m\otimes dn.

    Every element has finite support along the cohomological diagonal. The mapping complex instead has

    Homr⁡(M,N)=∏iHom⁡(Mi,Ni+r),d(f)=dNf−(−1)rfdM.\operatorname{Hom}^{r}(M,N) =\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(M^i,N^{i+r}), \qquad d(f)=d_Nf-(-1)^rf d_M.

    A homogeneous map must specify a map on every input degree; the product records that requirement. If Mi=Ni=ℂM^i=N^i=\mathbb C for all integers ii, with zero differentials, then degree zero of the tensor complex contains a direct sum indexed by ℤ\mathbb Z, whereas degree zero of the mapping complex is a product indexed by ℤ\mathbb Z. Replacing either by the other changes the complex even in this elementary example.

    A topology makes a further distinction. Put the discrete topology on each copy of ℂ\mathbb C. Every continuous linear functional

    ∏i≥0ℂ⟶ℂ\prod_{i\geq0}\mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb C

    depends on finitely many coordinates. Continuity makes its kernel contain a basic neighbourhood on which only finitely many coordinates are constrained. By contrast, an algebraic functional on ⨁iℂ\bigoplus_i\mathbb C can assign an arbitrary coefficient to every basis vector. Thus passing from a direct sum to a product and then taking a continuous dual can recover a direct sum. This conclusion depends on the displayed topology and on the discrete target.

    These examples explain why “take the dual” does not completely specify an operation for a field-theoretic construction. One must name the topology, the scalar ring and the degree totalization. The convention for shifts throughout this chapter is V[1]n=Vn+1V[1]^n=V^{n+1}.

    8.3 Laurent series with algebraic coefficients

    For a vector space VV over a field FF, define

    V((q))=⋃N∈ℤqNV[[q]].V((q))=\bigcup_{N\in\mathbb Z}q^N V[[q]].

    An element has one lower Laurent bound and an arbitrary sequence of coefficients in VV. If V=⨁j≥0FejV=\bigoplus_{j\geq0}Fe_j, then

    v(q)=∑j≥0qjejv(q)=\sum_{j\geq0}q^j e_j

    is allowed: each coefficient has finite support. There is no requirement that all coefficients lie in one finite-dimensional subspace of VV. Consequently

    V⊗FF((q))⊊V((q))V\otimes_F F((q))\subsetneq V((q))

    for this VV. A vector in the left side is a finite sum of Laurent series multiplied by fixed vectors of VV, so all its coefficients lie in one finite-dimensional subspace. The series v(q)v(q) does not.

    For a cochain complex, Laurent completion here means (V((q)))n=Vn((q))(V((q)))^n=V^n((q)), degree by degree. Its lower bound may depend on nn. If another product index is present, its lower bounds require a separate decision. For example, the family (q−r)r≥0(q^{-r})_{r\geq0} belongs to

    ∏r≥0F((q)),\prod_{r\geq0}F((q)),

    but not to (∏r≥0F)((q))(\prod_{r\geq0}F)((q)): the latter requires a lower bound common to all coordinates. In the current complex below, the product index includes exterior arity. Requiring one lower bound across every arity would discard valid cochains.

    There is also an order of scalar extension. Let

    A0=ℂ[λ,λ−1,(λ−1)−1],F=ℂ(λ).A_0=\mathbb C[\lambda,\lambda^{-1},(\lambda-1)^{-1}], \qquad F=\mathbb C(\lambda).

    The series ∑n≥2qn/(λ−n)\sum_{n\geq2}q^n/(\lambda-n) belongs to F[[q]]F[[q]]. It does not lie in A0[[q]]⊗A0FA_0[[q]]\otimes_{A_0}F. An element of this algebraic localization has a common denominator in A0A_0, whereas no one denominator clears the distinct poles λ=n\lambda=n. Scalar extension before completion therefore permits more series than algebraic localization afterwards.

    These distinctions also govern continuity. Multiplication by a fixed Laurent polynomial has a finite loss of qq-order. A family of operations is continuous on a completed direct sum only if the required bound applies before its support is allowed to grow. A bound depending on bar length, for instance, need not suffice when bar length grows with the Laurent exponent.

    8.4 The line algebra and its spectral tensor

    We now apply these conventions to a concrete comparison. Let

    𝔤=𝔰𝔩2(ℂ),κ(E,F)=1,κ(H,H)=2,k∈ℂ∖ℚ.\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C),\qquad \kappa(E,F)=1,\quad\kappa(H,H)=2,\qquad k\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Q.

    The affine mode algebra A=A−k−2A=A_{-k-2} has relations

    [xtr,yts]=[x,y]tr+s+rδr+s,0(−k−2)κ(x,y)1.[xt^r,yt^s]=[x,y]t^{r+s} +r\delta_{r+s,0}(-k-2)\kappa(x,y)1.

    Put 𝔫=t𝔤[t]\mathfrak n=t\mathfrak g[t], U=U(𝔤)U=U(\mathfrak g), and W=A⊗U(𝔫)ℂW=A\otimes_{U(\mathfrak n)}\mathbb C. A smooth affine module is one in which every vector is annihilated by all sufficiently high positive modes; the bound can depend on the vector.

    The differential graded line algebra Y=YkY=Y_k of Chapter 6 has even current generators BnaB_n^a and odd generators ca,nc_{a,n}, for n≥0n\geq0. The latter have cohomological degree one. Their internal energies are nn and n+1n+1, respectively; energy is a separate grading. To recall their concrete meaning, the induced Chevalley resolution

    P−p=A⊗Λp𝔫P^{-p}=A\otimes\Lambda^p\mathfrak n

    carries right operators Bna↦Rtat−n−atat−nB_n^a\mapsto R_{t_at^{-n}}-a_{t_at^{-n}} and ca,n↦ιa,n+1c_{a,n}\mapsto\iota_{a,n+1}. Here RR is right multiplication, axa_x is the exterior derivation obtained by projecting [x,−][x,-] to 𝔫\mathfrak n, and ιa,n+1\iota_{a,n+1} contracts the indicated positive mode. The differential of YY is compatible with these operators. They represent line operations on the boundary resolution, including the odd operations that would be lost by keeping only ordinary endomorphisms. The full presentation and its energy-restricted endomorphism comparison are given in Line operators and the boundary derived functor, §“Lifts of the line generators.”

    For ordinary, possibly unbounded, left YY-modules M,NM,N, form the algebraic tensor complex T=M⊗NT=M\otimes N. Let q=z−1q=z^{-1}. The spectral tensor has underlying complex T((q))T((q)), but its differential includes the interaction

    Sz(T)=(T((q)),dT+ρT(r(q))),S_z(T)=\bigl(T((q)),d_T+\rho_T(r(q))\bigr),
    r(q)=∑a,i,j≥0(−1)i(i+ji)qi+j+1(ca,i⊗Bja−Bia⊗ca,j).r(q)=\sum_{a,i,j\geq0}(-1)^i\binom{i+j}{i}q^{i+j+1} \bigl(c_{a,i}\otimes B_j^a-B_i^a\otimes c_{a,j}\bigr).

    The invariant form contracts the Lie indices. Every coefficient is a finite algebraic operator, and every term has positive qq-order. Write dYd_Y for the differential of YY. On the tensor-product algebra (Y⊗Y)((q))(Y\otimes Y)((q)), let QQ be the induced differential

    Q(a⊗b)=dYa⊗b+(−1)|a|a⊗dYb,Q(q)=0,Q(a\otimes b)=d_Ya\otimes b+(-1)^{|a|}a\otimes d_Yb, \qquad Q(q)=0,

    8.5 The incoming bar, its completion, and the outgoing bar

    The bar construction from Chapter 5 resolves the incoming module relations. Write 𝐁=Y⊗Y\mathbf B=Y\otimes Y. Its length-rr term is

    The tensor diagonals and bar lengths are summed before completion. At a fixed Laurent coefficient there are finitely many words and finitely many tensor-diagonal components. Those finite supports can grow with the exponent.

    The original augmentation ℬz(T)→Sz(T)\mathcal B_z(T)\to S_z(T) is a quasi-isomorphism. Its mechanism is instructive. Before the correction, insertion of a unit gives a contracting homotopy hh of Laurent order zero. Perturbing by δ=Lr(q)\delta=L_{r(q)} gives a homotopy of the form

    H=h(1+δh)−1=h∑j≥0(−δh)j.H=h(1+\delta h)^{-1} =h\sum_{j\geq0}(-\delta h)^j.

This proves convergence on the specified complex without interchanging an inverse limit with a bar realization. The projection remains the original augmentation. See Rational evaluation on the completed incoming bar, Proposition 1.

    The smooth realization is a different operation. For the specified smooth affine–right-YY object 𝒲\mathcal W, put

    ΦK(V)=𝒲K⊗YK𝕃V,K=ℂ((q)).\Phi_K(V)=\mathcal W_K\otimes^{\mathbb L}_{Y_K}V, \qquad K=\mathbb C((q)).

    The evaluation map is fixed on these bars. If pp is an outgoing rational-current resolution word, it sends

    p⊗b0[b1|⋯|br]t⟼Δrat(p)b0[b1|⋯|br]t.p\otimes b_0[b_1|\cdots|b_r]t \longmapsto \Delta_{\rm rat}(p)b_0[b_1|\cdots|b_r]t.

Its Laurent loss depends on pp, uniformly in the incoming length, letters and terminal vector. A vector in the outgoing algebraic bar uses finitely many such pp, so their bounds have a common minimum. Its restriction along the affine resolution is the original affine evaluation, usually denoted bM,Nb_{M,N}; the rational evaluation is denoted ηM,N\eta_{M,N}. Their construction precedes the theorem that they induce an equivalence.

All displayed products are retained. This definition comes from current operations and their support conditions, independently of smooth realization.

    Let D𝒩(AK)D_{\mathcal N}(A_K) be the full subcategory of the original smooth derived category whose cohomology has jointly locally nilpotent positive currents: each cohomology vector is killed by all sufficiently long products of positive currents. Its maps are the ambient derived maps.

    Theorem — finite radial current comparison. Assume the specified coherent smooth affine–right-YY realization, its tensor–Hom adjunction and full unit for ordinary unbounded YY-modules, its algebraic cofree model and common mode-cutoff actions. Assume also that every bounded-below smooth complex with jointly locally nilpotent positive-current cohomology belongs to the localizing category generated by WKW_K, and that the derived ideal triangle expresses each YFY_F-module by two complexes inflated from UFU_F. Here inflation uses the augmentation YF→UFY_F\to U_F, and the localizing category is closed under shifts, cones and arbitrary coproducts. Then, for every finite d≥2d\geq2, every ordinary unbounded tuple M1,…,MdM_1,\ldots,M_d, and every X∈D𝒩(AK)X\in D_{\mathcal N}(A_K), the actual evaluation gives an equivalence

At the regular tuple it retains all dd incoming regular right actions. Its coefficient evaluations are the rational maps ηM1,…,Md\eta_{M_1,\ldots,M_d} and their original affine restrictions bM1,…,Mdb_{M_1,\ldots,M_d}. The theorem uses the bar and scalar-extension orders stated above. See The radial finite-puncture current recipient, equation (45).

    The proof begins with inputs inflated from UFU_F, so the ghosts act by zero. The proper-current complex then contracts at order zero by the energywise dual of the free Chevalley contraction. Cross-point terms have positive Laurent order and increase mode support by at most that order. Perturbation therefore preserves the required support. Composed with this contraction, the actual comparison is 1+A1+A, with AA of positive order, and has a coefficientwise geometric inverse.

    For bounded-below inputs, representability and the positive-current torsion theorem extend this calculation to every ambient test in D𝒩D_{\mathcal N}. Explicit truncation towers then handle unbounded inflated inputs; their componentwise stabilization does not require a bound uniform over the product factors of ℐd\mathcal I_d. Finally, the two inflated terms of the ideal triangle extend the equivalence to one arbitrary input at a time. There are finitely many such steps. No infinite incoming bar is moved through a continuous Hom, and no equality D𝒩=Loc⁡(WK)D_{\mathcal N}=\operatorname{Loc}(W_K) is required.

    8.7 Finite integral heads and separated values

    There is a second useful route to the regular comparison. Before inverting the separation discriminant, one can work over Rd=ℂ[a1,…,ad−1]R_d=\mathbb C[a_1,\ldots,a_{d-1}]. The protected coefficient complex is generated by seeds Δw𝒞w⊗d\Delta^w\mathscr C_w^{\otimes d}, where Δ=∏i<j(ai−aj)\Delta=\prod_{i<j}(a_i-a_j) and 𝒞w\mathscr C_w is the energy-ww relative dual of the line algebra. The discriminant powers compensate the pole budgets. Closing these seeds under the specified currents and derivatives gives actual integral coefficient and current-chain complexes.

    A finite head bounds top energy, proper pole budget and derivative order. Each such head is a bounded perfect relative complex, so its derived dual commutes with derived scalar base change. After separation, normalized head duals assemble into the explicit complex

    Dˆn=(⨁N(DN0)n)((q))⊕︎(⨁N(DN0)n−1)((q)),\widehat D^n= \left(\bigoplus_N(D_N^0)^n\right)((q)) \oplus\left(\bigoplus_N(D_N^0)^{n-1}\right)((q)),
    d(f,g)=(dDf,(RNfN+1−qfN)N−dDg).d(f,g)=\bigl(d_Df,(R_Nf_{N+1}-qf_N)_N-d_Dg\bigr).

    Here DN0D_N^0 is the normalized head dual and RNR_N its restriction matrix after removing the common q−1q^{-1} factor. This formula specifies finite head support at every coefficient and one common lower Laurent bound. It does not use the unrestricted algebraic dual of the infinite head union.

    Evaluation is the original tensor–Hom map

    η(p⊗f)(l)=(−1)|p||f|f(p⊗l).\eta(p\otimes f)(l)=(-1)^{|p||f|}f(p\otimes l).

    For fixed pp, insertion changes the head NN to N+c(p)N+c(p). Normalization gives a Laurent loss depending on pp, independent of NN. Evaluation and its homotopies therefore extend to the completed head complexes. For the full incoming bar, the stronger estimate is uniform in incoming length, including arbitrarily long words of energy zero. These estimates identify the separated head construction with the same evaluation used above. The two occupied-vacuum orders also have actual completed comparison roofs at the regular output test, retaining the surviving regular action. See Integral kernels and the separated comparison diagrams, §§1–3.

    This separation of domains has a geometric consequence. A collision fibre sets a factor of Δ\Delta to zero, whereas the separated Laurent chart has inverted Δ\Delta. Derived collision maps are obtained from the integral finite heads before that inversion. They cannot be obtained by substituting a collision into every vector of the separated Laurent complex.

    8.8 Common radial sewing and a failed substitution

    The finite-point theorem permits a definite form of sewing: the original kernels can be composed along any finite binary tree on the same radial domain. The translation τx\tau_x of the source algebra YY is defined on either generator yn=Bnay_n=B_n^a or yn=ca,ny_n=c_{a,n} by

    τx(yn)=∑m=0n(nm)xn−mym,\tau_x(y_n)=\sum_{m=0}^n\binom nm x^{n-m}y_m,

    and extended multiplicatively. For fixed modes its kernel identities are rational identities,

    (τx⊗1)r(y)=r(y+x),(1⊗τx)r(y)=r(y−x).(\tau_x\otimes1)r(y)=r(y+x),\qquad (1\otimes\tau_x)r(y)=r(y-x).

    Continue those coefficients rationally before expanding radially. Each pair of leaves first meets at one vertex, so the tree contributes each term of R𝐚R_{\mathbf a} exactly once. Associative principal-part splitting gives the same rational and affine evaluations on the common completed incoming bar.

    A separately completed nested tensor need not have that domain. In a three-point shape chart,

    f=∑n≥0qnλ−n2∈ℂ(λ)((q)).f=\sum_{n\geq0}q^n\lambda^{-n^2}\in\mathbb C(\lambda)((q)).

    The substitution λ=zq\lambda=zq would give

    ∑n≥0z−n2qn−n2.\sum_{n\geq0}z^{-n^2}q^{n-n^2}.

    Its outer qq-orders have no lower bound, so it is not in ℂ((z−1))((q))\mathbb C((z^{-1}))((q)). The terms tend to zero before substitution and fail to do so afterwards. This is an obstruction to extending that substitution continuously to the entire radial field. It leaves the common radial sewing theorem intact and identifies the extra support estimate needed for a larger nested domain.

    Three rational poles and a finite-total spectator

    A separately completed pair-first operation has an actual comparison when its intermediate rational currents are retained. Fix the nonrational 𝔰𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_2 setting of this chapter and write

    a1=z+w,a2=z,a3=0,p=w−1,q=z−1,Kw=ℂ((p)),KN=Kw((q)).a_1=z+w,\quad a_2=z,\quad a_3=0, \qquad p=w^{-1},\quad q=z^{-1}, \qquad K_w=\mathbb C((p)),\quad K_N=K_w((q)).

    on the entire three-pole resolution. The rational intermediate resolution retains the extra pole missed by the affine cluster resolution. Full-source tensorator.

    The bar comparison gives a full-source derived evaluation into the original binary target. Its affine inclusion is a quasi-isomorphism in the original two-pole current category, and restriction recovers the original binary evaluation. This does not put a new strict three-pole action on the literal old complex. The further evaluation from the rational-cluster target to the triple target is not asserted to be a quasi-isomorphism.

    For a constant input T=T12⊗ℂM3T=T_{12}\otimes_{\mathbb C}M_3, distinguish the joint intermediate object from the factorized one:

    E=Sw12(T),E1=Sw(T12)⊗ℂM3,c:E1⟶E.E=S_w^{12}(T),\qquad E_1=S_w(T_{12})\otimes_{\mathbb C}M_3, \qquad c:E_1\longrightarrow E.

Under the chapter's retained coherent native realization and full-unit hypotheses, the full three-pole evaluation then reaches the independently factorized endpoint, preserving affine restriction and the native outgoing unit. Strict commutativity holds in the displayed algebraic bar models; smooth replacement retains the enhanced comparison and its specified coherences. A fixed left comb admits stagewise comparisons when each newly attached spectator has finite-total cohomology. Finite dimension in each degree does not suffice. Finite-total native comparison.

    There are two separate limits to this result. For trivial first inputs and third input given by the regular U=U(𝔰𝔩2)U=U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)-module, inflated along Y→UY\to U,

    E/E1=U((p))/(U⊗ℂKw)≠0E/E_1=U((p))/(U\otimes_{\mathbb C}K_w)\ne0

    with zero differential. For example ∑n≥0pnHn\sum_{n\geq0}p^n H^n, where HH is the Cartan generator of UU, has one algebraic coefficient at every inner order. Its coefficients span an infinite-dimensional space, so it survives in the quotient. This disproves the unrestricted equivalence of the two intermediate objects under cc. A comparison of evaluations can still use maps from a common domain, as the following construction shows.

    A common domain for the factorized intermediate object

    The regular spectator requires a comparison with the actual separately completed object. This comparison has an algebraic domain determined by the two carriers. Put s=q/p=w/zs=q/p=w/z, so that the substitution q=spq=sp identifies Kw((q))K_w((q)) with Kw((s))K_w((s)), and set

    LDfac(T)=LD(T)∩N1(T)=LR(T)∩N1(T).L_D^{\mathrm{fac}}(T)=L_D(T)\cap N_1(T)=L_R(T)\cap N_1(T).

    Degree by degree, for each outer exponent jj, its sjs^j-coefficient belongs to T12((p))⊗M(j)T_{12}((p))\otimes M^{(j)} for some finite-dimensional graded subspace M(j)⊂M3M^{(j)}\subset M_3. The subspace may grow with jj, but it works for the entire inner pp-series at that outer coefficient. This condition makes the intersection a dg YDY_D-module and gives actual maps

    LR(T)⟵LDfac(T)⟶N1(T).L_R(T)\longleftarrow L_D^{\mathrm{fac}}(T)\longrightarrow N_1(T).

    The construction preserves quasi-isomorphisms in each input. The outgoing action and factorwise incoming actions preserve it; a general commuting endomorphism of the joint input need not preserve finite spectator support. The factorized common domain.

    If H∙(M3)H^\bullet(M_3) has finite total dimension, the canonical inclusion LDfac(T)→LD(T)L_D^{\mathrm{fac}}(T)\to L_D(T) is a quasi-isomorphism. A contraction of the underlying spectator complex to its finite cohomology suffices; no line-module structure on that auxiliary cohomology is required. The cross perturbation has positive order in both pp and ss, so only finitely many spectator operators contribute at each fixed outer order. Both domains retract onto the same transferred complex. Their raw comparison cones consequently agree with the joint-domain cones. They need not vanish: at trivial input they are KR/DK_R/D and KN/DK_N/D. Finite-total comparison and its cones.

    Theorem (three-pole evaluation). The entire three-pole rational current resolution has an evaluation on a resolved model for LDfac(T)L_D^{\mathrm{fac}}(T). The theorem holds for arbitrary constant ordinary dg inputs, in particular the regular triple Y⊗3Y^{\otimes3}. Let M=T12M=T_{12}, N=M3N=M_3, A=Y⊗2A=Y^{\otimes2} and B=YB=Y. Resolve the two inputs separately by the augmented bars

    RM=BarA⁡(A,M),RN=BarB⁡(B,N).R_M=\operatorname{Bar}_A(A,M),\qquad R_N=\operatorname{Bar}_B(B,N).

    Write F3(V,W)F_3(V,W) for the underlying array intersection just defined, with VV in the completed pair and WW in the spectator position. With the pair-sum twist on its free heads, F3(RM,RN)F_3(R_M,R_N) augments by a quasi-isomorphism to LDfac(T)L_D^{\mathrm{fac}}(T). For the evaluation target, replace the free right heads in the two bars by P⊗2P^{\otimes2} and PP, respectively. Call the resulting bars TM,TNT_M,T_N. Their ordinary bar differentials give F3(TM,TN)F_3(T_M,T_N) its differential.

    For a resolved rational current word π\pi, expand Δ(3)(π)\Delta^{(3)}(\pi) in the three affine heads. The direct expansion gives algebraic rational rows with common lower bounds. The factorization Δ(3)=(Δ(12)⊗1)Δ(12|3)\Delta^{(3)}=(\Delta^{(12)}\otimes1)\Delta^{(12|3)} gives a second estimate. Each outer coefficient uses finitely many third heads, and applying the inner tensorator leaves them fixed. The two estimates put the same kernel in F3(P⊗2,P)F_3(P^{\otimes2},P). Its action on a pair of bar words is

    η(π;x⊗y)=Δ(3)(π)⋅(x⊗y) ∈F3(TM,TN).\eta(\pi;x\otimes y)=\Delta^{(3)}(\pi)\cdot(x\otimes y)\ \in F_3(T_M,T_N).

    The dot multiplies the heads and retains all letters and both terminal vectors, with the tensor signs. At each outer order a finite convolution of finite spectator spans suffices. The bound depends on the resolved word and the output order and permits arbitrarily long horizontal words in the incoming bars. In the chain identity the right twist of Δ(3)\Delta^{(3)} cancels the twist of the free heads. This explains the ordinary differential in the target.

    There are two comparisons of this map. On the radial side, shuffle the two algebraic bars. The signed interleavings cancel the faces that multiply letters from different bars, and leave head multiplication intact. On the pair-first side, form the actual outer binary bar after Sw(RM)⊗RNS_w(R_M)\otimes R_N and use its augmentation and the separate augmentations of RM,RNR_M,R_N. On outer length zero apply the inner tensorator to the rational pair head. The two length-one faces cancel by its right-linearity. These maps give the radial and pair-first evaluations with their affine restrictions and specified endpoint units. They use no inverse of E1→EE_1\to E. A further theorem would have to realize the common-domain adjunction unit as a universal class in an independently constructed smooth current complex on every admitted test.

    Part of the recipient can also be built directly from currents. Divide the exterior proper modes between the first pair and the spectator, keeping the restricted dual of each exterior power. At each fixed outer exponent require the third-slot modes, their cofree coefficients and the spectator input to span a finite space through the inner series. The current differential preserves this requirement. An action internal to the pair leaves the third slot fixed, and a term crossing into it with kernel order hh costs at least shs^h. Only finitely many such orders contribute to a fixed outer coefficient. This gives a subcomplex on constant smooth tests and the usual proper-current evaluation on every regular word, including arbitrary horizontal UU-words. Identifying its full smooth action on general tests with the common-domain adjunction is the remaining representability question.

    The topology can be seen directly from the coefficients. Give LR(T)L_R(T) its radial pp-adic topology and N1(T)N_1(T) its outer ss-adic topology. Each coefficient has discrete topology at its respective stage. In their product, equality of every pisjp^is^j coefficient defines a closed subspace, the graph of LDfac(T)L_D^{\mathrm{fac}}(T). It is complete, and its two projections have dense images. To approximate a common array in both topologies, take all rows below a radial cutoff and all columns below an outer cutoff, then subtract the finite rectangle counted twice. Whole columns retain finite spectator support. For v≠0v\ne0, the sequence pnvp^n v already distinguishes the two endpoints. It tends to zero radially and has constant outer order zero. Thus continuity on the common graph gives no continuous extension of the identity from the entire radial input to the native pair-first input.

    Tests over a coefficient ring

    The common ring DD is not a field, and an ordinary Hom formula can detect a choice of test representative. Let g=p+sg=p+s. Substitution p=−sp=-s maps DD to ℂ((s))\mathbb C((s)) and kills gg, so gg is a nonunit. The complex

    E=(D→gD⟶D/g),E0=D,E1=D,E2=D/g,E=(D\xrightarrow{g}D\longrightarrow D/g), \qquad E^0=D,\quad E^1=D,\quad E^2=D/g,

    is acyclic, but H0HomD⁡(E,D)=D/g≠0H^0\operatorname{Hom}_D(E,D)=D/g\ne0. Let WDW_D be the scalar extension to DD of the regular-top affine object in the tensor–Hom realization. For trivial incoming coefficient, the ordinary current formula on the acyclic smooth test WD⊗DEW_D\otimes_D E retracts onto this nonacyclic Hom complex. Thus that formula cannot define the proposed functor on arbitrary derived DD-tests. The field and constant ground-field test theorems retain their stated scope. The ordinary-Hom counterexample.

    A positive comparison holds on explicit finite WDW_D-cell models: bounded complexes formed from WDW_D by finitely many shifts, finite sums and cones, with their actual enhanced maps. Finite cone induction extends the comparison at WDW_D, and proves invariance under quasi-isomorphisms between these models. This includes the finite induced Chevalley model of the parameter-Verma family. A value on an arbitrary representative, or on every object generated by unrestricted coproducts, requires a derived test construction and its support theorem. Finite cell tests.

    Two independently completed clusters

    Part III Operations and their domainsChapter 9 of 18

    9

    Ordered boundary operations and mixed theories

    Moving one insertion past another can change an operation even when the fields vary smoothly. The ordering region has a boundary, and differentiating its indicator produces a current on that boundary. When the insertions also have a holomorphic separation, this real boundary can meet a complex pole. The resulting contact term belongs to the operation.

    The problem is therefore more precise than extending a formula to coincident points. We need a space of distributions on which the formula, its differential and its compositions are all defined. We also need to distinguish a collision in the complex coordinate from a collision in both the real and complex coordinates. These distinctions lead to the relative complexes and height homotopies in this chapter.

    9.1 A boundary current from a mixed field theory

    On M=ℂz×ℝ≥0,tM=\mathbb C_z\times\mathbb R_{\geq0,t}, let

    d′=∂‾+dt,∂=dz∧∂z.d'=\bar\partial+d_t,\qquad \partial=dz\wedge\partial_z.

    A holomorphic–topological theory is holomorphic in zz and topological in the real direction. In its cohomological description, the antiholomorphic and real derivatives enter d′d'; holomorphic derivatives remain genuine operations.

    An abelian example has fields (α,β)(\alpha,\beta), where α\alpha is a form generated by dz‾,dtd\bar z,dt, while β\beta has one additional factor dzdz. An ordinary form of degree pp in either summand has cohomological degree p−1p-1. The differential is

    Qκ(α,β)=(d′α,d′β+κ∂α).Q_\kappa(\alpha,\beta) =\bigl(d'\alpha,d'\beta+\kappa\partial\alpha\bigr).

    Since d′∂+∂d′=0d'\partial+\partial d'=0, its square is zero for every κ\kappa. The degree-zero fields are the partial connection aa and holomorphic one-form bb. Their quadratic action density is

    ℒκ=b∧d′a+κ2a∧∂a.\mathcal L_\kappa=b\wedge d'a+\frac{\kappa}{2}a\wedge\partial a.

    At κ=0\kappa=0, this is the holomorphic BF presentation: the field bb multiplies the partial curvature F=d′aF=d'a.

    The integrated action requires compact support. The Batalin–Vilkovisky pairing pairs the two field summands by wedge product and integration and is independent of κ\kappa. This pairing includes the odd ghost and antifield components of the complex; retaining only a,ba,b would omit the differential needed for the quantum identities.

    Impose the boundary condition ι∗α=0\iota^*\alpha=0, with β\beta free at the boundary. A compactly supported contraction in the normal direction identifies the boundary observables with their supported bulk realization. This is an instance of the free bulk–boundary construction of Gwilliam, Rabinovich and Williams, Factorization algebras and abelian CS/WZW-type correspondences (arXiv:2001.07888). With residue integration normalized by (2πi)−1∫(2\pi i)^{-1}\int, the resulting current has singular product

    J(z)J(w)∼−ℏκ(z−w)2.J(z)J(w)\sim-\frac{\hbar\kappa}{(z-w)^2}.

    At κ=0\kappa=0, that singular product vanishes, but the bulk pairing is still nondegenerate and all polynomial current fields and holomorphic jets remain. Thus the level of a boundary current is not the same datum as the nondegeneracy of the bulk field pairing. The construction and signs are developed in Holomorphic BF theory and its boundary current, particularly the theorems on the boundary map and current at every level.

    9.2 Fields as joint currents

    The boundary calculation fixes a local operator product. A distributional current model makes the support data for moving and composing such operations explicit. On the full space ℝ×ℂ\mathbb R\times\mathbb C, write XI=(ℝ×ℂ)IX_I=(\mathbb R\times\mathbb C)^I for the external insertion positions. The variables in the coefficient distributions remain independent, even when two external points coincide.

    This coefficient complex has two polarizations, called xx and pp. An internal mixed form of degree rr has cohomological degree r−2r-2 in the xx-polarization and r−1r-1 in the pp-polarization. On every compact set of external parameters, the xx-variables have a common compact support. A pp-variable can extend upward in height, but above a common collar height its current is independent of that height and has no dtdt-component. This is the meaning of upward-proper support here. Particle number is finite, and these finite operations are defined over ℂ[ℏ]\mathbb C[\hbar].

    On one coefficient variable, the internal differential is

    Q(fx)=(d′f)x,Q(gp)=−(d′g)p,δ(fx)=−(∂zf)p,δ(gp)=0.Q(f_x)=(d'f)_x,\qquad Q(g_p)=-(d'g)_p,\qquad \delta(f_x)=-(\partial_zf)_p,\qquad \delta(g_p)=0.

    With external forms placed first, the full differential is

    𝒟=dXI+Q+δ,(Q+δ)(ω⊗n)=(−1)|ω|ω⊗(Q+δ)n.\mathcal D=d_{X_I}+Q+\delta, \qquad (Q+\delta)(\omega\otimes n) =(-1)^{|\omega|}\omega\otimes(Q+\delta)n.

    The notation dXId_{X_I} denotes the mixed exterior derivative in the position variables. The coefficient differential and its shifts are part of this formula.

    At position ii, Wˆi\widehat W_i integrates the pp-field on the upward ray, pˆi\widehat p_i evaluates that field at the endpoint, and the degree-zero current Jˆi\widehat J_i combines the xx-point field with the holomorphic derivative of the ray. They obey

    𝒟Wˆi=−pˆi,𝒟pˆi=𝒟Jˆi=0.\mathcal D\widehat W_i=-\widehat p_i,\qquad \mathcal D\widehat p_i=\mathcal D\widehat J_i=0.

    They are smooth families of distributions in the internal variables. Normal ordering means multiplication in independent internal variables followed by particle symmetrization. It introduces no extra contraction at coincident external endpoints.

    For nij=(tj−ti,zi−zj)n_{ij}=(t_j-t_i,z_i-z_j), the nonzero cross contractions are

    ⟨Wi,Jj⟩=−ℏb1(nij),⟨pi,Jj⟩=ℏQ1(nij),⟨Ji,Jj⟩=ℏE2(zi−zj).\langle W_i,J_j\rangle=-\hbar b_1(n_{ij}),\qquad \langle p_i,J_j\rangle=\hbar Q_1(n_{ij}),\qquad \langle J_i,J_j\rangle=\hbar E_2(z_i-z_j).

    Here Em(z)E_m(z) is the principal-value current z−mz^{-m}, QmQ_m is a scalar one-form kernel, and, off z=0z=0,

    b1(t,z)=12z(1+tt2+|z|2).b_1(t,z)=\frac{1}{2z} \left(1+\frac{t}{\sqrt{t^2+|z|^2}}\right).

    The height distinguishes the two sides of a complex collision. At positive height its singular part approaches 1/z1/z; at negative height it becomes regular near z=0z=0.

    A scalar distribution KK of finite order multiplies a smooth coefficient family FF by the joint-test formula

    ⟨KF,φ⟩=⟨K, q⟼⟨F(q),φ(q,⋅)⟩⟩.\langle KF,\varphi\rangle =\left\langle K,\ q\longmapsto \langle F(q),\varphi(q,\cdot)\rangle\right\rangle.

    Uniform support, collar and finite-order estimates make this a joint distribution. In particular, a relation between two expressions is an equality after all external and internal tests. A graph presentation is a way to compute the current, not additional data attached to it. This distinction is what permits the product in Composition on actual Gaussian images and their finite contact strata to accept its earlier output as a new input.

    9.3 Ordered poles and their complete differential

    Let H(t)H(t) be the Heaviside distribution and set

    rm(z)=π(−1)m−1(m−1)!∂zm−1δℂ(z)dz‾,Cm(t,z)=δ(t)dt∧rm(z).r_m(z)=\frac{\pi(-1)^{m-1}}{(m-1)!} \partial_z^{m-1}\delta_{\mathbb C}(z)\,d\bar z, \qquad C_m(t,z)=\delta(t)\,dt\wedge r_m(z).

    Thus ∂‾Em=rm\bar\partial E_m=r_m. The first bulk kernel is the distributional one-form represented off the origin by

    Q1(t,z)=z‾2(t2+|z|2)3/2dt−t4(t2+|z|2)3/2dz‾.Q_1(t,z)= \frac{\bar z}{2(t^2+|z|^2)^{3/2}}\,dt -\frac{t}{4(t^2+|z|^2)^{3/2}}\,d\bar z.

    bm=(−1)m−1(m−1)!∂zm−1b1,Qm=(−1)m−1(m−1)!∂zm−1Q1.b_m=\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\partial_z^{m-1}b_1, \qquad Q_m=\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\partial_z^{m-1}Q_1.

    Dbm=Qm+H(t)rm,DQm=−Cm,D=dt+∂‾.D b_m=Q_m+H(t)r_m,\qquad DQ_m=-C_m, \qquad D=d_t+\bar\partial.

    The term H(t)r1H(t)r_1 is the distributional contribution at the complex pole. Differentiating it gives C1C_1, which cancels DQ1DQ_1. This is the full identity D2b1=0D^2b_1=0. Omitting the real wall would destroy it.

    With many rays, the whole arrangement must be extended across its dependent collision loci. Multiplying independently extended factors on a common singular normal need not define a distribution. The scalar arrangement kernels use the following extension class.

    Work on a coordinate space V=Vt×VzV=V_t\times V_z, with VtV_t real and VzV_z complex. Let ℒ\mathscr L be the finite intersection-closed lattice of proper subspaces generated by the complex collision loci, mixed collision loci and gate walls. Its members are products of real-linear and complex-linear subspaces. At y∈Vy\in V, let L(y)L(y) be the intersection of the lattice members containing yy, or VV if there are none, and let πy:V→V/L(y)\pi_y:V\to V/L(y) be the quotient. If its real factor has dimension pyp_y and its complex factor has complex dimension kyk_y, the quotient has mixed dimension py+kyp_y+k_y.

    A normal current ω\omega is bihomogeneous of bidegree (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) if, including its form factors,

    gλ,θ∗ω=λαeiβθω,gλ,θ(t,z)=(λt,λeiθz),λ>0.g_{\lambda,\theta}^*\omega =\lambda^\alpha e^{i\beta\theta}\omega, \qquad g_{\lambda,\theta}(t,z)=(\lambda t,\lambda e^{i\theta}z), \quad\lambda>0.

    Its excess is α−β\alpha-\beta. A current is tame if near each yy it has a finite presentation

    ∑jηj∧πy∗ωj,\sum_j\eta_j\wedge\pi_y^*\omega_j,

    where ηj\eta_j are smooth mixed forms and ωj\omega_j are bihomogeneous normal currents of nonnegative excess. It is subcritical if, at every point of the lattice union, these models can be chosen with deg⁡ωj<py+ky\deg\omega_j<p_y+k_y. This bounds the normal model degree, which can be smaller than the total degree after multiplication by ηj\eta_j. The whole scalar arrangement has a unique extension in this class agreeing with its regular kernel; see Subcritical Q cycles and finite native Gaussian kernels, equation (1.4), Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 3.2. This fixes the scalar extension; a physical principle selecting that extension is a separate question.

    A supporting flat is described by a partition of the real coordinates and a partition of the complex coordinates. Compatibility means that the real partition refines the complex one: equality in height is imposed only within a complex block. Scalar rays and marked one-forms QmQ_m join distinct complex blocks. Gates H(h)H(h) compare real blocks inside a complex block. One also allows finite holomorphic derivatives of the top normal delta currents.

    For a set AA of marked edges, let pAp_A be the real rank of its height forms and kAk_A the complex rank of its complex forms. The nonzero admissible case requires |A|<pA+kA|A|<p_A+k_A for every nonempty marked subset; violating this inequality gives the zero whole kernel. A critical contact has

    |A|=pA+kA−1.|A|=p_A+k_A-1.

    The two ranks can differ. For example, Q1(s,u)∧Q1(t,u)Q_1(s,u)\wedge Q_1(t,u) has two independent real normals and one complex normal. With

    Ω2=πδ(s)δ(t)δℂ(u)ds∧dt∧du‾,\Omega_2=\pi\delta(s)\delta(t)\delta_{\mathbb C}(u) \,ds\wedge dt\wedge d\bar u,

    the complete gated current satisfies

    D[H(t−s)Q1(s,u)∧Q1(t,u)]=−12∂uΩ2.D\bigl[H(t-s)Q_1(s,u)\wedge Q_1(t,u)\bigr] =-\frac12\partial_u\Omega_2.

    The factor 1/21/2 is determined by the two complementary chambers. Their currents sum to the ungated current, whose derivative is −∂uΩ2-\partial_u\Omega_2; interchanging s,ts,t makes their two coefficients equal. This computation never assigns a value to H(0)H(0). A ray weight changes the residue: on the corresponding whole arrangement,

    D[Q1(s,u)∧Q1(t,u)b1(s,u)]=14∂u2Ω2.D\bigl[Q_1(s,u)\wedge Q_1(t,u)b_1(s,u)\bigr] =\frac14\partial_u^2\Omega_2.

    These formulas illustrate the weighted normal theorem, rather than multiplication of an existing point contact by a singular ray.

    Let ℳI\mathcal M_I be the actual finite span of these compatible scalar currents multiplied by finite normally ordered W,p,JW,p,J families and smooth external forms, including all allowed holomorphic normal jets. The following closure theorem is the basic algebraic input to moving the operations.

    Theorem — finite marked Ward calculus. With the stated compatible flats, internal gates, finite pole and jet orders, upward-proper coefficient support and canonical scalar extension, 𝒟ℳI⊆ℳI\mathcal D\mathcal M_I\subseteq\mathcal M_I. For a scalar coefficient KK with qq marked factors, its derivative consists of four finite sums:

    DK=ℬ(K)+𝒮(K)+𝒱(K)+𝒞(K).DK=\mathcal B(K)+\mathcal S(K)+\mathcal V(K)+\mathcal C(K).

    Here ℬ\mathcal B replaces a ray by an additional mark with sign (−1)q(-1)^q; 𝒮\mathcal S takes the residues of entire complex-parallel scalar classes; 𝒱\mathcal V takes the oriented real boundaries of whole simplified gates; and 𝒞\mathcal C is the sum over closed critical marked flats. Its coefficients are the annular moments of the whole weighted, gated normal kernel. The derivative of KFKF also includes (−1)qK𝒟F(-1)^qK\mathcal DF. Old normal degrees contribute their Koszul sign, and every residue differentiates the entire remaining coefficient and field family to the required finite normal order.

    The proof classifies all active normal strata. Removing an entire vanishing scalar class leaves proper tangent factors; the critical-normal calculation supplies the missing mixed contacts. Finite-order estimates justify each transpose against a joint test. Since the formula equals the actual distributional differential, it respects every relation between presentations of the same current. The precise statement is The finite marked Ward calculus on compatible collision flats, Theorems 4.1 and 7.1.

    The disjoint-label Gaussian product ⋆\star also closes on this space and is associative with its labelled signs. Its Ward defect

    𝔚(X,Y)=𝒟(X⋆Y)−(𝒟X)⋆Y−(−1)|X|X⋆(𝒟Y)\mathfrak W(X,Y)=\mathcal D(X\star Y) -(\mathcal DX)\star Y-(-1)^{|X|}X\star(\mathcal DY)

    is computable from the same formulas and is supported on cross complex collisions. Consequently 𝒟\mathcal D is not a derivation of this product. The defect is retained as operation data.

    9.4 Relative currents and a radial homotopy

    9.5 Changing endpoint profiles

    A normal contraction also depends on a compact profile. Let pp integrate along an interval and let sa,sbs_a,s_b be sections defined by normalized profiles θa,θb\theta_a,\theta_b. Then

    Tba=1+(sb−sa)p,TcbTba=Tca,Tab=Tba−1.T_{ba}=1+(s_b-s_a)p,\qquad T_{cb}T_{ba}=T_{ca},\qquad T_{ab}=T_{ba}^{-1}.

    This transports the entire source and root map, not only their cohomology classes. A quantum operation must also transport its local pairing.

    For a planar disk DD and interval II, take the endpoint coefficient complex ℰc=Ωc∙(D×I)[2]\mathcal E_c=\Omega_c^\bullet(D\times I)[2] with b(u,v)=ν∫u∧vb(u,v)=\nu\int u\wedge v, with ν≠0\nu\ne0. Put A=(sb−sa)pA=(s_b-s_a)p and T=1+AT=1+A. Since both AuAu and AvAv contain dtdt,

    This defect can be nonzero. Choose a compact planar function ϕ\phi, a compact planar two-form ψ\psi, and real distinct profiles, with ∫Dϕψ≠0\int_D\phi\psi\ne0. For u=ϕ(θb−θa)u=\phi(\theta_b-\theta_a) and v=ψθadtv=\psi\theta_a\,dt, it equals
