    15.3 A faithful ordinary comparison on a K3 surface

    There is a compact example in which the flags themselves can be compared. Choose a smooth projective complex K3 surface SS with an ample polarization HH, H2=8H^2=8, and divisor classes D1,D2,D3,VD_1,D_2,D_3,V whose Néron–Severi lattice has matrix

    (−8−4−41−4−8−41−4−4−821120),H=D3+4V.\begin{pmatrix} -8&-4&-4&1\\ -4&-8&-4&1\\ -4&-4&-8&2\\ 1&1&2&0 \end{pmatrix},\qquad H=D_3+4V.

    The period construction supplies such a polarized surface: the lattice has signature (1,3)(1,3), and H⟂H^\perp contains no class of square −2-2. Set Li=𝒪S(Di)L_i=\mathcal O_S(D_i). They are HH-Gieseker stable with the common Hilbert polynomial χ(Li(mH))=4m2−2\chi(L_i(mH))=4m^2-2, and satisfy

    dim⁡Ext∙⁡(Li,Li)=(1,0,1),dim⁡Ext∙⁡(Li,Lj)=(0,2,0)(i≠j).\dim\operatorname{Ext}^\bullet(L_i,L_i)=(1,0,1), \qquad \dim\operatorname{Ext}^\bullet(L_i,L_j)=(0,2,0)\quad(i\ne j).

    Let 𝒜L\mathcal A_L be their finite-extension category in the abelian category of semistable sheaves of the fixed reduced Hilbert polynomial. All its objects and subquotients are vector bundles.

    The surface and polarization are part of this construction; arbitrary triples of spherical bundles need not have the same reduced Hilbert polynomial. A common-polynomial spherical triple

    The independent algebraic category is that of finite-dimensional nilpotent left modules over a completed preprojective algebra Πˆ\widehat\Pi. Start with three vertices and two arrows on each chosen oriented pair; double the arrows and impose the preprojective moment relation at each vertex. If JJ is the arrow ideal, a module is nilpotent when JNM=0J^NM=0 for some finite NN. Completion of the path algebra does not turn such a module into an infinite-dimensional object.

    Take the ordinary Hall algebras of rational constructible functions, and within them the unital composition subalgebras 𝒞Π\mathcal C_\Pi and 𝒞L\mathcal C_L generated by the three simple indicators. The distinction is useful: the theorem identifies these entire generated algebras, rather than merely checking a few relations, but does not assert an isomorphism of every constructible function on the two moduli problems.

    Theorem (ordinary K3 Hall comparison). Choose the simultaneous cyclic minimal A∞A_\infty model of the collection and a comparison with its Dolbeault category strictly unital over the quiver vertex-idempotent algebra ℂ3\mathbb C^3. There is a unique unital, charge-graded isomorphism

    Θ:𝒞Π→∼𝒞L\Theta:\mathcal C_\Pi\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal C_L

    sending the simple indicator at vertex ii to 1[Li]1_{[L_i]}. At every finite nilpotence bound it comes from an algebraic tensor family. Over reduced bases this family identifies reduced relative flag varieties, their subquotients, and all forgetting and regrouping maps. Primitive recognition, Proposition “Regular families and the ordinary composition algebra”

    The proof explains why the result reaches flags. In the minimal model, the differential is zero. For an operation mkm_k with k≥3k\ge3, a degree-zero input is a vertex unit, so strict unitality kills the operation. A degree-two input with the remaining inputs positive would force the output above degree two. With all inputs in degree one, cyclicity pairs the output against a unit; strict unitality again makes it zero. The perfect cyclic pairing then forces the output itself to vanish. The remaining quadratic equation is precisely the preprojective moment relation.

    At nilpotence bound NN, the comparison applied to a module involves only paths shorter than NN. Applied to the regular module of Πˆ/JN\widehat\Pi/J^N, it gives an algebraic bundle with a right action of that finite-dimensional algebra. Tensoring this bundle with a module family preserves exact sequences and base change. The resulting flag comparison makes every Hall word have the same value on corresponding objects. The two word-evaluation maps therefore have the same kernel, which proves faithfulness as well as surjectivity.

    An independent action on completed Enriques cycle states satisfies all six real Serre relations. That action can have a kernel while Θ\Theta remains faithful: a faithful identification of algebras and a faithful representation of that algebra are different assertions. This distinction will matter again when an algebra is represented on a space of compact states.

    15.4 Critical coefficients and orientation

    On a Calabi–Yau threefold, the local deformation theory of an object is governed by its self-extension complex. A critical chart presents the moduli problem as the critical locus of a function ff on a smooth space. Its vanishing-cycle complex records the topology of nearby fibres of ff; replacing it by its Euler characteristic discards cohomological degree and parity.

    To glue these local coefficient complexes one needs an orientation: a square root of the appropriate determinant line, together with its squaring map. In the determinant convention used here, write

    KF=det⁡RHom⁡(F,F),D(F,G)=det⁡RHom⁡(F,G),JF⊗2≃KF.K_F=\det R\operatorname{Hom}(F,F),\qquad D(F,G)=\det R\operatorname{Hom}(F,G),\qquad J_F^{\otimes2}\simeq K_F.

    An extension requires compatible root maps involving JF⊗JG⊗D(F,G)J_F\otimes J_G\otimes D(F,G). The cross determinant D(F,G)D(F,G) is part of the map. Its Euler-characteristic sign is not a replacement for the line itself.

    For critical coefficient complexes 𝒫α\mathscr P_\alpha, the extension correspondence must carry an actual morphism

    p∗(𝒫α⊠𝒫β)⟶q!𝒫α+β.p^*(\mathscr P_\alpha\boxtimes\mathscr P_\beta) \longrightarrow q^!\mathscr P_{\alpha+\beta}.
    (15.2)

    Here q!q^! is exceptional inverse image, the duality-compatible pullback. By adjunction, (15.2) gives a map after q!q_!; on a proper middle map this is the usual proper pushforward. The chosen cohomology theory, support convention and degree shifts must make this push-pull operation well defined. Associativity asks that its two composites agree on the actual three-step flag, with the orientation identifications included.

    The first framed charge-two example shows what the geometric comparison must retain. A flag for framed instanton data includes an invariant line. In a chart let uu be the difference of the two support positions and DD the slope of that line. Restriction of the matrix moment equation to the curve, after eliminating two regular pairs, gives the coefficient

    Kf=R′[D]⊗Λ(η,χ),|η|=|χ|=−1,dη=uD,dχ=0.K_f=R'[D]\otimes\Lambda(\eta,\chi),\qquad |\eta|=|\chi|=-1,\qquad d\eta=uD,\quad d\chi=0 .

    Here one can take R′=ℂ[t1,t2,β±1,κ,z,w,q]/(q4)R'=\mathbb C[t_1,t_2,\beta^{\pm1},\kappa,z,w,q]/(q^4), u=z−wu=z-w. The parameters t1,t2t_1,t_2 are the two equivariant weights, β\beta sets the scale, and qq records the order of the deformation. The closed odd variable comes from a fourth moment equation whose value on the flag is identically zero. Replacing KfK_f by the equation uD=0uD=0 would discard it.

    The classical equation has two branches, D=0D=0 and u=0u=0. Their constant coefficient glues along their common origin by the difference of the two restrictions. Both branches occur with multiplicity +1+1 in the oriented transverse graph. The second branch contributes integration with compact support along DD before the Thom map for u=0u=0. On the field side one can already construct the supported Cauchy coefficient. After removing its invertible exchange factor, its first cubic representative is

    2t1t2(t1+t2)q3β−3(z−t)−3(t−w)−1.2t_1t_2(t_1+t_2)q^3\beta^{-3}(z-t)^{-3}(t-w)^{-1}.

    Taking the first-current coefficient at the auxiliary point t=wt=w gives 2t1t2(t1+t2)q3β−3u−32t_1t_2(t_1+t_2)q^3\beta^{-3}u^{-3}. Multiplication by u2u^2 detects this simple residue.

    There is a sharp way to test how much normal information a lift needs. Impose the two equations up=D=0u^p=D=0, and write Mp=R′[D]/(up,D)M_p=R'[D]/(u^p,D). In the Cauchy coefficient TT of finite principal parts, uu lowers pole order and kills u−1u^{-1}. On the moment complex C=T[D]⊗Λ(η,χ)C=T[D]\otimes\Lambda(\eta,\chi), with dη=uDd\eta=uD, a map Mp→H0(C)=TM_p\to H^0(C)=T may send 11 to any m∈ker⁡upm\in\ker u^p. It lifts to a derived linear map Mp→CM_p\to C exactly when up−1m=0u^{p-1}m=0. Indeed, resolve the two equations by Koszul generators and lift mm through the DD face by ηt\eta t, where ut=mut=m. The remaining face, evaluated at D=0D=0, requires upt=up−1m=0u^pt=u^{p-1}m=0. Conversely, raising the order of each pole in mm by one gives such a tt and a lift with zero last face. Thus the nonzero cubic pole has no lift on the third normal cut, and a lift on the fourth. On that fourth cut it also lifts to the original rational Cauchy representatives with both odd actions retained. This test has a prescribed auxiliary source M4⊗ΛχM_4\otimes\Lambda\chi.

    What remains open is a map of the same variance on the whole flag which carries the proper oriented operation to the field operation. It must act on both odd directions, the framing line, the two branches and their common restriction, agree with both vacuum maps and compose on refined flags. In particular it must supply a geometric input for the cubic representative just calculated.

    There is a strong orientation theorem on a specific compact domain. Let X=SKum×EX=S_{\mathrm{Kum}}\times E, with a Calabi–Yau volume form, and choose a smooth elliptic fibre C⊂SKumC\subset S_{\mathrm{Kum}}, points p∈Cp\in C, x∈Ex\in E, and L∈Pic0⁡(E)L\in\operatorname{Pic}^0(E). The actual semi-topological components of

    A=𝒪C⊠𝒪x,B=𝒪p⊠LA=\mathcal O_C\boxtimes\mathcal O_x, \qquad B=\mathcal O_p\boxtimes L

    generate a subgroup Γ≅ℤ2\Gamma\cong\mathbb Z^2. Here a semi-topological component is a connected-component class in the moduli of perfect complexes, with addition induced by direct sum. Deformation in a connected family preserves this class; equality of numerical Chern characters need not identify component classes. On the union of these components, the compact orientation root admits unital associative root maps for every finite ordered flag, without changing its square. The two isomorphism classes of enhancements form an H2(Γ,𝔽2)H^2(\Gamma,\mathbb F_2)-torsor. Strong orientation on compact two-charge components

    The mechanism is concrete. The ratio between two triple root maps is a sign, and the pentagon makes these signs a group three-cocycle. Since a two-torus is a classifying space for ℤ2\mathbb Z^2, its third cohomology vanishes; correcting the binary maps by a two-cochain removes the defect. The use of actual components is essential. The theorem does not identify them with every object of the same numerical charge, nor does it provide equivariant descent or compare the root with a separately chosen geometric orientation.

    Parity remains visible throughout. For example, 2929 even and 9393 odd directions have superdimension −64-64, just as 6464 purely odd directions do. The scalar −64-64 determines neither the graded vector space nor its bracket. A proposed identification with an automorphic denominator algebra must compare these coefficients and operations, not only their alternating counts.

    15.5 Compact reduction keeps relative moment values

    A particularly explicit domain consists of sheaves

    J(T)=𝒪S⊠TJ(T)=\mathcal O_S\boxtimes T

    on S×ES\times E, where TT has finite length on EE. Put Cn=Coh0n⁡(E)C_n=\operatorname{Coh}_0^n(E). Its self-extension theory on the threefold is

    RHomS×E⁡(J(T),J(T′))≃RHomE⁡(T,T′)⊗(ℂ⊕︎ℂη),|η|=2,η2=0.R\operatorname{Hom}_{S\times E}(J(T),J(T')) \simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_E(T,T') \otimes(\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C\eta), \qquad |\eta|=2,\quad\eta^2=0.

    The adjective spherical refers here to the two scalar self-extension groups of 𝒪S\mathcal O_S, in degrees zero and two. The second summand carries the paired obstruction directions. The classical CnC_n is smooth, but (15.3) is not just its ordinary tangent complex. The flag domain requires every associated graded factor to lie in this spherical sector; constraining only the middle object admits extra subobjects.

    For every n>0n>0, let 𝔘n\mathfrak U_n be the derived sheaf open with classical objects J(T)J(T), and fix a point x∗∈Sx_*\in S. Write r∗=Lix∗∗r_*=Li_{x_*}^* for restriction to {x∗}×E\{x_*\}\times E, and let pS,pEp_S,p_E be the projections of S×ES\times E. The four reduction maps have types

    det⁡V:𝔘n⟶B𝔾m,V(F)=RΓ(E,r∗F),mnr∗:𝔘n⟶E,μE:𝔘n⟶𝔸[−1],μsc:𝔘n⟶𝔸[−2].\begin{aligned} \det V &: \mathfrak U_n\longrightarrow B\mathbb G_m, &V(F)&=R\Gamma(E,r_*F),\\ m_nr_* &: \mathfrak U_n\longrightarrow E,\\ \mu_E &: \mathfrak U_n\longrightarrow\mathbb A[-1], &\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}&:\mathfrak U_n\longrightarrow\mathbb A[-2]. \end{aligned}

    Here B𝔾mB\mathbb G_m classifies line bundles, mn(T)m_n(T) is the support sum with multiplicities, and 𝔸[−j]=𝕍(ℂ[−j])\mathbb A[-j]=\mathbb V(\mathbb C[-j]) is a derived additive group, rather than an ordinary affine line. The map μE\mu_E is minus the logarithm of det⁡RpS∗F\det Rp_{S*}F, normalized by its value at x∗x_*. Its line is classically trivial and rigidified at that point; the K3 volume form identifies its derived logarithm with 𝔸[−1]\mathbb A[-1]. The second moment uses the similarly rigidified relative determinant detX⁡F⊗pE∗(detE⁡r∗F)−1\det_XF\otimes p_E^*(\det_Er_*F)^{-1}; elliptic Serre integration gives its logarithm in 𝔸[−2]\mathbb A[-2].     The root-space question also has an independent mathematical answer on its own algebra. In the parity-minimal Gritsenko–Nikulin algebra the signed denominator in the doubled coordinate is D5(2Z)D_5(2Z). At the sum of the three real simple roots the signed coefficient is −64-64, while the presentation gives 2929 even and 9393 odd states. Two even three-generator brackets survive Jacobi and 2727 more come from bracketing a real and a null generator. The chamber correction supplies 9393 odd simple generators. An auxiliary space with 6464 odd states gives the same signed coefficient. Lifting the denominator from such numbers to a compact Hall algebra requires both parity dimensions, the primitive bracket, its relations and a compatible action on the state space.

    The same requirement applies to a Hall-to-field comparison. On a declared charge, coefficient and support domain, the map must carry the coefficient morphism (15.2) to the specified position-dependent field operation. Its three-input compatibility is an equality or a specified homotopy on the full flag/configuration correspondence. The target must contain the actual shifted singular divisors and normal directions; agreement of generator relations or scalar characters does not define this map. A prepared state is further data: a distinguished vector or functional with specified gluing laws, not an arbitrary normalization chosen to reproduce one trace.

    Period and isogeny constructions supply additional genuine comparisons. Rational marked isogeny transport preserves the Hilbert-state ring and pairing, and the primitive marked relative tensors in the stated effectiveness chambers with one reduced sewing factor. An integral Brauer-twisted Fourier–Mukai endpoint changes rank and degree, so its relative operation problem belongs to the corresponding twisted higher-rank moduli. These maps constrain a realization, but do not identify its full coefficient, orientation and prepared-state systems automatically. Period and isogeny state comparison

    A trace theorem therefore has a definite place in the construction: it is what results when an already defined operation is closed. Arithmetic will present the same distinction in another form. A functional may count every spectral multiplicity exactly while its pairing, positive realization and local operations remain separate mathematical questions.

    Part IV Geometric and arithmetic realizationsChapter 16 of 18

    16

    Arithmetic traces and positivity

    A trace formula compares two descriptions of the same functional. One description sums spectral contributions; the other is assembled from geometric or arithmetic operations. In statistical mechanics, a trace such as Tr⁡(e−tH)\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-tH}) counts energy levels with multiplicity. In arithmetic, the explicit formula for the Riemann zeta function relates its zero divisor to prime powers and the real place. The analogy becomes a mathematical construction only when the spaces, operators and trace domains are defined independently of the spectral answer.

    Several such arithmetic objects can be constructed. They retain integer summation, Fourier transform, full multiplicity jets and even a geometric realization of the complete explicit-formula trace. The stronger questions concern positivity and local operations: can the full functional arise from an ordinary positive star representation, and can its arithmetic operations be compared with local fields while preserving collisions, units and integral normal directions? A scalar trace identity answers neither question by itself.

    16.1 The complete arithmetic functional

    Use logarithmic scale u=log⁡xu=\log x, so multiplication of positive scales becomes addition. For a test f∈Cc∞(ℝ)f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R), set

    fˆ(z)=∫ℝf(u)eizudu,Hf(s)=∫ℝf(u)e(s−1/2)udu=fˆ(−i(s−1/2)).\widehat f(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(u)e^{izu}\,du, \qquad H_f(s)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(u)e^{(s-1/2)u}\,du =\widehat f(-i(s-1/2)).

    Convolution and involution are

    (f∗g)(u)=∫f(t)g(u−t)dt,f∗(u)=f(−u).(f*g)(u)=\int f(t)g(u-t)\,dt, \qquad f^*(u)=\overline{f(-u)}.

    The complete Weil functional, in this normalization, is

    W(f)=Hf(0)+Hf(1)−f(0)log⁡π+12π∫ℝfˆ(r)Re⁡ψ(1/4+ir/2)dr−∑n≥2Λ(n)n(f(log⁡n)+f(−log⁡n)),\begin{aligned} W(f)={}&H_f(0)+H_f(1)-f(0)\log\pi\\ &+\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(r) \operatorname{Re}\psi(1/4+ir/2)\,dr\\ &-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n} \bigl(f(\log n)+f(-\log n)\bigr), \end{aligned}
    (16.1)

    where ψ=Γ′/Γ\psi=\Gamma'/\Gamma, Λ(pk)=log⁡p\Lambda(p^k)=\log p, and Λ(n)=0\Lambda(n)=0 otherwise. The first two terms are the polar contributions, the integral is part of the real-place contribution, and the last sum contains both orientations of every prime power. For instance, each of f(log⁡4)f(\log4) and f(−log⁡4)f(-\log4) has coefficient −log⁡2/2-\log2/2, since 4=224=2^2. The test algebra and its scalar functional

    The completed zeta function

    ξ(s)=12s(s−1)π−s/2Γ(s/2)ζ(s)\xi(s)=\tfrac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)

    is entire. Let ρ\rho run through its distinct zeros, let mρm_\rho be the multiplicity, and write wρ=−i(ρ−1/2)w_\rho=-i(\rho-1/2). The explicit formula identifies (16.1) with

    W(f)=∑ρmρfˆ(wρ).W(f)=\sum_\rho m_\rho\widehat f(w_\rho).
    (16.2)

    The decay of the transform and the zero-counting bound give convergence on the stated test class. Formula (16.1), however, can be defined without knowing any zero individually. This distinction is the starting point for a geometric trace construction.

    Positivity concerns the quadratic form

    Q(g)=W(g∗g∗).Q(g)=W(g*g^*).
    (16.3)

    Since g∗g∗ˆ(z)=gˆ(z)gˆ(z‾)\widehat{g*g^*}(z)=\widehat g(z)\overline{\widehat g(\bar z)}, a real wρw_\rho contributes mρ|gˆ(wρ)|2m_\rho|\widehat g(w_\rho)|^2. A nonreal point does not contribute an absolute square. The Weil positivity criterion equates Q(g)≥0Q(g)\ge0 for every compact smooth complex test with the Riemann hypothesis. Thus the all-test quantifier is part of the mathematical problem, not a harmless extension of a finite calculation.

    16.2 Multiplicity, nilpotence and two different pairings

    Before constructing an infinite-dimensional arithmetic space, consider the finite algebra

    Am=ℂ[z]/(zm).A_m=\mathbb C[z]/(z^m).

    For a=a0+a1z+⋯+am−1zm−1a=a_0+a_1z+\cdots+a_{m-1}z^{m-1}, multiplication MaM_a is triangular in the monomial basis, with diagonal a0a_0. Hence

    Tr⁡Ma=ma0,Btr(a,b)=Tr⁡Mab=ma0b0.\operatorname{Tr}M_a=ma_0, \qquad B_{\mathrm{tr}}(a,b)=\operatorname{Tr}M_{ab}=ma_0b_0.

    The trace counts the length mm, but its associated pairing has radical (z)(z). All nilpotent directions disappear from that pairing.

    The residue functional gives a different answer:

    res⁡(a)=[zm−1]a,Bres(a,b)=[zm−1](ab).\operatorname{res}(a)=[z^{m-1}]a, \qquad B_{\mathrm{res}}(a,b)=[z^{m-1}](ab).

    For m=3m=3, the two pairing matrices in 1,z,z21,z,z^2 are

    Btr=(300000000),Bres=(001010100).B_{\mathrm{tr}}= \begin{pmatrix}3&0&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad B_{\mathrm{res}}= \begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\0&1&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
    (16.4)

    The residue matrix has determinant −1-1, so it is perfect. It is a complex-bilinear duality, not a positive Hermitian inner product. Already over the real subalgebra, Bres(1−z2,1−z2)=−2B_{\mathrm{res}}(1-z^2,1-z^2)=-2.

    If N=MzN=M_z and A=ρI+NA=\rho I+N, then

    etA=etρ∑j=0m−1tjNjj!,Tr⁡(etA)=metρ.e^{tA}=e^{t\rho}\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\frac{t^jN^j}{j!}, \qquad \operatorname{Tr}(e^{tA})=me^{t\rho}.

    The trace retains multiplicity but does not determine the Jordan chain. Nor does putting weight mm on one point of a measure space create mm independent operator-trace coordinates. These elementary distinctions recur in the arithmetic complex: a full zero divisor, a perfect residue dual and a positive Hilbert representation encode different information.

    There is also a sharp conditional constraint. If a Hilbert-space generator satisfies A∗=1−AA^*=1-A on its full equal adjoint domain, then A−12A-\tfrac12 is skew-adjoint. Its spectral values lie on the imaginary axis, and no nontrivial finite Jordan chain can lie in that domain. Such an adjoint identity would therefore impose both a critical-line condition and a restriction on nilpotent jets. A continuous duality alone does not supply it. Integer-summation middle complex, duality and primary blocks

    16.3 Integer summation defines the complex before its spectrum

    Let S=𝒮(ℝ)evenS=\mathscr S(\mathbb R)^{\mathrm{even}}, and impose the two Poisson boundary conditions

    S00={ϕ∈S:ϕ(0)=0, ∫ℝϕ=0}.S_{00}=\{\phi\in S:\phi(0)=0,\ \int_{\mathbb R}\phi=0\}.

    For n≥2n\ge2, define

    En={f:en⟨x⟩f∈Hn(ℝ)},E=⋂n≥2En,⟨x⟩=(1+x2)1/2,E_n=\{f:e^{n\langle x\rangle}f\in H^n(\mathbb R)\}, \qquad E=\bigcap_{n\ge2}E_n, \qquad \langle x\rangle=(1+x^2)^{1/2},

    with its projective-limit Fréchet topology. Equivalently, the derivatives of an element of EE decrease faster than every exponential at both ends. The arithmetic complex is

    Cℤ=[S00→ZE],(Zϕ)(x)=2∑m≥1ϕ(mex),C_{\mathbb Z}=[S_{00}\xrightarrow{Z}E], \qquad (Z\phi)(x)=2\sum_{m\ge1}\phi(me^x),
    (16.5)

    in cohomological degrees zero and one.

    Why do these two boundary conditions occur? For the Fourier transform ℱϕ(v)=∫ϕ(u)e−2πiuvdu\mathcal F\phi(v)=\int\phi(u)e^{-2\pi iuv}\,du, Poisson summation gives

    Zϕ(x)=e−xZℱϕ(−x)+e−x∫ϕ−ϕ(0).Z\phi(x)=e^{-x}Z\mathcal F\phi(-x) +e^{-x}\int\phi-\phi(0).
    (16.6)

    Schwartz decay controls +∞+\infty; (16.6) controls −∞-\infty once the two displayed boundary terms vanish. The two excluded functionals themselves form the polar lines, with dilation characters zero and one. They have not been inserted from a list of zeros.

    To define the adelic averaging, let 𝔸ℚ\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q} be the adele ring and Cℚ=𝔸ℚ×/ℚ×C_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q}^{\times}/\mathbb Q^{\times} its idele class group. The modulus |c||c| is the product of the normalized local absolute values. Its kernel C1C^1 is compact; over ℚ\mathbb Q, it identifies with ℤˆ×\widehat{\mathbb Z}^{\times}, where ℤˆ=∏pℤp\widehat{\mathbb Z}=\prod_p\mathbb Z_p. Give C1C^1 Haar measure of mass one and put

    (PF)(c)=∫C1F(kc)dk,(ΣΦ)(c)=∑q∈ℚ×Φ(qc).(PF)(c)=\int_{C^1}F(kc)\,dk, \qquad (\Sigma\Phi)(c)=\sum_{q\in\mathbb Q^{\times}}\Phi(qc).

    Here Φ\Phi is an adelic Schwartz–Bruhat test: Schwartz at the real place and locally constant with compact support at the finite places. Impose Φ(0)=∫𝔸ℚΦ=0\Phi(0)=\int_{\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q}}\Phi=0, with finite additive volume vol⁡(ℤˆ)=1\operatorname{vol}(\widehat{\mathbb Z})=1. For Φ=ϕ⊗1ℤˆ\Phi=\phi\otimes1_{\widehat{\mathbb Z}}, finite-place integrality selects exactly the nonzero integers, and (PΣΦ)(ex)=Zϕ(x)(P\Sigma\Phi)(e^x)=Z\phi(x). This is the averaging map in the following theorem.

    Theorem (continuous integer-summation duality). The map ZZ is a closed topological embedding. Its quotient M=E/Z(S00)M=E/Z(S_{00}) is complete and nuclear. Norm-one adelic averaging identifies the actual averaged pole-free lattice-summation image with Z(S00)Z(S_{00}). Under the Mellin transform, that image is exactly the ideal of functions vanishing at every zero of ξ\xi to its full multiplicity. At each weighted Sobolev stage, the annihilator is the norm closure of the full dualizing-jet functionals at the same stage. Their inductive limit gives the strong continuous dual. Evaluation yields a nondegenerate hypocontinuous pairing: continuity is uniform when either argument ranges over a bounded set. It extends through the specified tensor completion formed using bounded sets. An integer-summation middle complex and its continuous dual

    The first step of the proof is arithmetic inversion, after removing the factor of two in ZZ. On logarithmic weighted spaces with exponent σ>1\sigma>1, the operators

    ∑m≥1λ−log⁡m,∑m≥1μ(m)λ−log⁡m\sum_{m\ge1}\lambda_{-\log m}, \qquad \sum_{m\ge1}\mu(m)\lambda_{-\log m}

    converge in operator norm and are inverse; μ(m)\mu(m) is the Möbius function and λtϕ(u)=ϕ(e−tu)\lambda_t\phi(u)=\phi(e^{-t}u). Fourier reflection then controls both ends and gives inverse continuity in Schwartz seminorms. This proves closed range before spectral synthesis is used.

    For Re⁡s>1\operatorname{Re}s>1, Mellin transformation gives ℳ(Zϕ)(s)=2ζ(s)∫0∞ϕ(u)usdu/u\mathcal M(Z\phi)(s)=2\zeta(s)\int_0^\infty\phi(u)u^s\,du/u. An explicitly differentiated Gaussian supplies an arithmetic convolution generator with Mellin transform ξ(s)\xi(s). Quantitative division on vertical strips, followed by Gaussian regularization, proves equality with the full vanishing ideal. The dual jet functionals are therefore genuine continuous functionals on the arithmetic quotient; no simplicity assumption removes their higher derivatives.

    The dual is complex-linear. To compare dilation characters, its contragredient action is tensored with the character ete^t: an exponent ρ\rho becomes 1−ρ1-\rho. This weight-one twist explains the reflection symmetry without turning the pairing into a positive inner product. The finite example (16.4) warns precisely against that inference.

    16.4 A geometric construction of the full trace

    For trace-class operators one needs explicit Hilbert domains. Fix a>1/2a>1/2, and use the convolution algebra

    𝒜a={f∈C∞(ℝ):pa,N(f)=∑j=0N∫ea|u||f(j)(u)|du<∞ for every N}.\mathcal A_a= \left\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R): p_{a,N}(f)=\sum_{j=0}^N\int e^{a|u|}|f^{(j)}(u)|\,du<\infty \text{ for every }N\right\}.

    It is a complete nonunital Fréchet star algebra. Its Fourier transforms are holomorphic in |Im⁡z|<a|\operatorname{Im}z|<a; on smaller strips they decrease faster than every power in the real direction. Compact smooth tests are dense. The identity for convolution would be the Dirac distribution, which is outside this function algebra.

    The arithmetic relation ideal in this test algebra is defined by normalized theta summation:

    θv(u)=eu/2∑n≥1v(neu)=12eu/2(Zv)(u),v∈S00,𝒥a={θv:v∈S00}𝒜a.\theta_v(u)=e^{u/2}\sum_{n\ge1}v(ne^u) =\tfrac12e^{u/2}(Zv)(u),\qquad v\in S_{00}, \qquad \mathcal J_a= \overline{\{\theta_v:v\in S_{00}\}}^{\,\mathcal A_a}.

    Poisson summation and the decay conditions place every θv\theta_v in 𝒜a\mathcal A_a; its closed image span is a convolution star ideal. Thus 𝒜a/𝒥a\mathcal A_a/\mathcal J_a is the quotient by specified arithmetic relations, with its Hausdorff quotient topology.

    Choose 1/2<s<min⁡(a,1)1/2<s<\min(a,1). The theta construction uses the Hilbert completion of even Schwartz functions in the norm

    ‖v‖𝒱s2=∫0∞x2s(|v(x)|2+|ℱv(x)|2)dx.\|v\|_{\mathscr V_s}^2 =\int_0^\infty x^{2s} \bigl(|v(x)|^2+|\mathcal Fv(x)|^2\bigr)\,dx.
    (16.7)

    Both boundary values v(0)v(0) and ℱv(0)\mathcal Fv(0) are continuous because s>1/2s>1/2. In logarithmic coordinates, combine the weighted spaces L2(e2sudu)L^2(e^{2su}du) and L2(e−2sudu)L^2(e^{-2su}du). The diagonal image and the paired theta/Fourier image are closed; their difference, by Poisson summation, spans exactly the two polar characters. This produces a two-term Hilbert complex 𝒞s=[V→dU]\mathscr C_s=[V\xrightarrow d U] in degrees −1,0-1,0, with dd bounded below, and theta quotient Ks=U/dVK_s=U/dV.

    Convolution acts strictly on the complex by ρf\rho_f. Choose a nonnegative even smooth bump bb, supported in [−1,1][-1,1], with integral one, and put ϕ(u)=∫−∞ub(v)dv\phi(u)=\int_{-\infty}^u b(v)\,dv. A bounded smoothing homotopy HfH_f, constructed using this cutoff, gives

    Λf=ρf−δHf,δT=dT−(−1)|T|Td.\Lambda_f=\rho_f-\delta H_f, \qquad \delta T=dT-(-1)^{|T|}Td.

    Each diagonal component of Λf\Lambda_f is trace class.

    Theorem (geometric theta trace). For every f∈𝒜af\in\mathcal A_a, the induced quotient operator Πs,a(f)\Pi_{s,a}(f) satisfies

    TrKs⁡Πs,a(f)=Str𝒞s⁡Λf=W(f),‖Πs,a(f)‖1≤Ca,s,ϕpa,4(f).\operatorname{Tr}_{K_s}\Pi_{s,a}(f) =\operatorname{Str}_{\mathscr C_s}\Lambda_f=W(f), \qquad \|\Pi_{s,a}(f)\|_1\le C_{a,s,\phi}p_{a,4}(f).
    (16.8)

    Here ϕ\phi is the fixed smoothing cutoff, and the supertrace is the degree-zero trace minus the degree-minus-one trace. A common Hilbert theta complex, geometric full trace

    The prime-power operators and the real-place Fourier defect are constructed before their traces are evaluated. The two-dimensional polar quotient contributes both polar terms. Trace-class cyclicity and the closed-image decompositions then give (16.8). No spectral expansion is used to define this complex or prove its complete trace formula.

    One can decide whether an equivalent Hilbert norm on this quotient would turn the convolution action into a star representation. Let Ut(s)U_t^{(s)} be translation by tt on KsK_s. At every 1/2<s<min⁡(a,1)1/2<s<\min(a,1) and every real t≠0t\ne0 its spectrum and its Fredholm essential spectrum both equal

    {λ∈ℂ:e−s|t|≤|λ|≤es|t|}.\{\lambda\in\mathbb C:e^{-s|t|}\le|\lambda|\le e^{s|t|}\}.

    In the strip model translation is the compression of multiplication by eitze^{itz} to the Hardy quotient by the inner factor of the theta divisor. This gives the outer and inner bounds by applying the multiplier estimate to tt and −t-t. For the reverse inclusion, arbitrarily large zero multiplicities counted over unit horizontal intervals can be moved into one box strictly inside the strip. Their translated inner factors then tend to zero on compact sets. The translated quotient projections tend strongly to the identity. Projecting a point-evaluation vector and translating it back gives unit vectors tending weakly to zero, on which the adjoint acts arbitrarily close to the conjugate of the corresponding multiplier value, up to a unit phase. These values fill the open annulus, and essential spectrum is closed.

    The outer radius exceeds one. Spectrum is preserved by an equivalent norm, whereas a unitary has spectrum on the unit circle. If the integrated tests gave a star representation in that norm, translating a real even approximate identity would make Ut(s)U_t^{(s)} unitary. Thus changing the norm within its equivalence class cannot produce the desired positive realization. The integrated smooth operators in (16.8) still have their full trace. The strip-width assumption is needed to put the entire translated zero box strictly inside the Hardy strip.

    16.5 The trace domain and its coherent multiplication

    The identity on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is not trace class. One should therefore expect a proper trace ideal, rather than a finite trace on every bounded operator. For 𝒞s=[V→U]\mathscr C_s=[V\to U], put

    ℑ0={(T−1,T0)∈𝔖1(V)⊕︎𝔖1(U):dT−1=T0d},ℑ−1=𝔖1(U,V).\begin{aligned} \mathfrak I^0&=\{(T^{-1},T^0)\in\mathfrak S_1(V)\oplus\mathfrak S_1(U): dT^{-1}=T^0d\},\\ \mathfrak I^{-1}&=\mathfrak S_1(U,V). \end{aligned}

    Here 𝔖1\mathfrak S_1 denotes trace-class operators. Composition and δ\delta make ℑ\mathfrak I a complete proper nonunital differential ideal of the bounded chain endomorphisms. Its closed graded trace is

    τ(T)=TrU⁡T0−TrV⁡T−1,τ(δK)=0.\tau(T)=\operatorname{Tr}_UT^0-\operatorname{Tr}_VT^{-1}, \qquad \tau(\delta K)=0.

    The last identity follows from Tr⁡(dK)=Tr⁡(Kd)\operatorname{Tr}(dK)=\operatorname{Tr}(Kd). Orthogonal splitting of the closed range of dd contracts this ideal onto 𝔖1(Ks)\mathfrak S_1(K_s) by a split differential-algebra quasi-isomorphism. The chain-map equation involves dd, whereas taking ordinary Hilbert adjoints involves d∗d^*; a positive differential-star structure does not follow. Trace-class coefficient homotopies

    The trace-class representatives multiply up to an actual trace-class homotopy:

    ΛfΛg−Λf∗g=δK(f,g).\Lambda_f\Lambda_g-\Lambda_{f*g}=\delta K(f,g).
    (16.9)

    The homotopy is obtained by applying the bounded inverse of dd on its closed range to the degree-zero defect. It also satisfies

    ΛfK(g,h)−K(f,g)Λh+K(f,g∗h)−K(f∗g,h)=0.\Lambda_fK(g,h)-K(f,g)\Lambda_h +K(f,g*h)-K(f*g,h)=0.
    (16.10)

    Products of two degree-minus-one homotopies vanish. Equations (16.9)–(16.10), with their mixed-degree versions, assemble into a coalgebra chain map on the bar construction. On a word, it sums over partitions into consecutive blocks of size one or two, applying Λ\Lambda to a singleton and KK to a pair. The triple identity is exactly the equality needed when a bar differential joins adjacent entries.

    This also has an analytic completion theorem. Using the arithmetic ideal 𝒥a\mathcal J_a defined above, form the coefficient complex ℰ=[𝒥a→𝒜a]\mathcal E=[\mathcal J_a\to\mathcal A_a] in degrees −1,0-1,0. Its degree-zero multiplication and action on 𝒥a\mathcal J_a are convolution; products of two degree-minus-one terms are zero. On tensor words use the completed projective seminorms

    PR,N(x)=∑n≥0RnqN,π(xn),R>0,P_{R,N}(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}R^nq_{N,\pi}(x_n),\qquad R>0,

    where qNq_N is the sum of the two coefficient seminorms. In this nonfactorial entire completion, the bar map is continuous with radius bound

    PRℑ(Gx)≤PC1R+C2R,4(x).P_R^{\mathfrak I}(Gx)\le P_{C_1R+\sqrt{C_2R},4}(x).

    The estimate counts the same singleton/pair partitions. It extends the actual identities, not just a scalar trace, through the specified completion.

    Locality asks for different structure. A supported coefficient can carry derivatives normal to a collision locus; a derived diagonal product also retains the classes measuring nontransverse intersection. Supported mapping complexes, such normal-jet sheaves, Gaussian preparation and completed finite-word comparisons are available. Their linking construction supplies a cyclic vector and nonlocal creation fields. It does not turn the linking algebra into a local field algebra.

    A finite matrix calculation makes two boundaries visible. On K⊕︎ℂΩK\oplus\mathbb C\Omega, extend an original operator by T⊕︎0T\oplus0. Then

    Tr⁡(T⊕︎0)=Tr⁡T,⟨Ω,(T⊕︎0)Ω⟩=0.\operatorname{Tr}(T\oplus0)=\operatorname{Tr}T, \qquad \langle\Omega,(T\oplus0)\Omega\rangle=0.

    Rank-one maps c(v)=|v⟩⟨Ω|c(v)=|v\rangle\langle\Omega| and a(w)=|Ω⟩⟨w|a(w)=|\Omega\rangle\langle w| can make Ω\Omega cyclic, but

    [a(w),c(v)]=⟨w,v⟩PΩ−|v⟩⟨w|[a(w),c(v)]=\langle w,v\rangle P_\Omega-|v\rangle\langle w|

    is generally nonzero. For constant fields, multiplying this commutator by any power of z−wz-w does not make it vanish. Cyclicity is not locality, and a cyclic vector state is not the counting trace. In the arithmetic linking construction, the original trace remains on the corner that annihilates the added invariant vector. Invariant vacuum and linking fields

    16.6 A positive representation and its exact missing remainder

    There is nevertheless an ordinary positive representation on the critical part of the divisor. Differences of polynomially weighted quotient traces define positive functionals

    σn(f)=∑γ∈ℝmγ≥nfˆ(γ),n≥1.\sigma_n(f)=\sum_{\substack{\gamma\in\mathbb R\\m_\gamma\ge n}} \widehat f(\gamma),\qquad n\ge1.

    Here γ\gamma ranges over the real centered zeros and mγm_\gamma is their multiplicity. Complete the test algebra modulo the null space of σn(f∗∗g)\sigma_n(f^**g), and call the resulting Hilbert space GnG_n. The direct sum Gcrit=⨁nGnG_{\mathrm{crit}}=\bigoplus_nG_n carries a continuous ordinary star representation

    πcrit:𝒜a/𝒥a⟶𝔖1(Gcrit),\pi_{\mathrm{crit}}:\mathcal A_a/\mathcal J_a\longrightarrow\mathfrak S_1(G_{\mathrm{crit}}),

    with

    Tr⁡πcrit(f)=∑γ∈ℝmγfˆ(γ).\operatorname{Tr}\pi_{\mathrm{crit}}(f) =\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbb R}m_\gamma\widehat f(\gamma).
    (16.11)

    A zero of multiplicity mm occurs in exactly mm layers. This is how multiplicity becomes ordinary trace multiplicity, rather than merely a scalar measure weight. The generator is self-adjoint on its declared weighted square-summability domain, and inverse moments of order at least two converge. Polynomial quotients, positive multiplicity layers

    The difference from (16.8) is explicit:

    W(f)−Tr⁡πcrit(f)=∑wρ∉ℝmρfˆ(wρ).W(f)-\operatorname{Tr}\pi_{\mathrm{crit}}(f) =\sum_{w_\rho\notin\mathbb R}m_\rho\widehat f(w_\rho).
    (16.12)

    Isolation of a nonreal spectral point shows that this remainder vanishes on every test exactly when all centered zeros are real. The positive construction does not prove that vanishing. Its estimates on products of test operators likewise do not create local collision maps.

    16.7 What integral arithmetic points forget

    Integral arithmetic has an analogous loss of information under scalar evaluation. Fix a prime pp, including two. A delta structure is encoded by a Frobenius lift φ\varphi through δ(x)=(φ(x)−xp)/p\delta(x)=(\varphi(x)-x^p)/p. On ℤp\mathbb Z_p, take φ=id\varphi=\mathrm{id}. At positive finite height h≥1h\ge1, put

    Ah=ℤp[x0,…,xh−1],Rh=lim←n⁡Ah/pn,Ih=(p,xip−xi:i<h),Bh=lim←n⁡Ah/Ihn.A_h=\mathbb Z_p[x_0,\ldots,x_{h-1}],\quad R_h=\varprojlim_nA_h/p^n,\quad I_h=(p,x_i^p-x_i:i<h),\quad B_h=\varprojlim_nA_h/I_h^n.

    The last ring is the formal completion along the finite-field rational locus, defined independently of any comparison image. For each c∈𝔽phc\in\mathbb F_p^h, choose the integer representatives 0≤ci<p0\le c_i<p in ℤp\mathbb Z_p. With these lifts, Chinese remainders give

    Bh≃∏c∈𝔽phℤp[[z0,…,zh−1]],xi=ci+zi.B_h\simeq\prod_{c\in\mathbb F_p^h}\mathbb Z_p[[z_0,\ldots,z_{h-1}]], \qquad x_i=c_i+z_i.
    (16.13)

    The natural jh:Rh→Bhj_h:R_h\to B_h is injective, also modulo every pnp^n: translation by cc is a polynomial automorphism, and polynomials inject into formal power series over the finite coefficient ring.

    Frobenius has the variance

    φh:Rh⟶Rh+1,xi⟼xip+pxi+1.\varphi_h:R_h\longrightarrow R_{h+1}, \qquad x_i\longmapsto x_i^p+px_{i+1}.

    It raises height. Its extension to Bh→Bh+1B_h\to B_{h+1} commutes with jj. At the arithmetic point aa, evaluate xix_i at δi(a)\delta^i(a). This evaluation commutes with Frobenius because (δia)p+pδi+1a=δia(\delta^i a)^p+p\delta^{i+1}a=\delta^ia; it does not preserve all normal operations.

    To define the normal operation, let Si(x,y)S_i(x,y) be the integral arithmetic addition polynomials, characterized by the free-jet identity Si(x,y)=δi(x0+y0)S_i(x,y)=\delta^i(x_0+y_0). The first two are

    S0=x0+y0,S1=x1+y1−(x0+y0)p−x0p−y0pp.S_0=x_0+y_0,\qquad S_1=x_1+y_1- \frac{(x_0+y_0)^p-x_0^p-y_0^p}{p}.

    The quotient polynomial is integral. Use independent divided-power parameters tit_i; their symbols ti[n]t_i^{[n]} satisfy ti[r]ti[s]=(r+sr)ti[r+s]t_i^{[r]}t_i^{[s]}=\binom{r+s}{r}t_i^{[r+s]}, so the construction does not invert factorials in ℤp\mathbb Z_p.     There is no weak uniform allowance hidden between the fixed theorem and the global question. The allowance ε(T)=max⁡(0,−λ(T))\varepsilon(T)=\max(0,-\lambda(T)) is nondecreasing; global boundedness, boundedness along one cofinal sequence, or subexponential growth already has Riemann-hypothesis strength. The unresolved signed Schur estimates must retain all prime, polar, real-place and tail contributions.

    The arithmetic problem consequently has several precise comparison maps. Continuous duality retains the full jets; the theta complex realizes the full trace; the positive critical construction leaves exactly (16.12); integral normal comparison retains (16.14); local fields require collision operations beyond the existing linking algebra. A reconstruction theorem must decide which of these structures it preserves and construct the corresponding map on its actual domain. That is the point at which arithmetic trace theory joins the general boundary-to-bulk questions of the next chapter.

    Part V Reconstruction and open problemsChapter 17 of 18

    17

    From boundary operations to bulk reconstruction

    The boundary reconstruction problem can now be stated without asking one invariant to carry several meanings. A local field algebra specifies position-dependent products. A category of representations specifies systems on which those products act. An interface specifies how to pass between two such categories. A state evaluates observables, while a geometric filling prepares a particular state with its amplitude and gluing law. Each construction has appeared in a concrete form in the preceding chapters.

    The central question is whether these constructions agree with ones defined independently in the bulk. There is no single comparison whose existence follows from the word holography. There are maps of observables, functors on representations, compatibility with products and collisions, and comparisons of states and amplitudes. Their hypotheses may overlap without coinciding. The strongest available reconstruction is obtained by composing the maps on their common domains and retaining the distinctions outside those domains.

    17.1 Interfaces give an explicit reconstruction map

    The ordinary algebraic model is useful because all its arrows can be written. Let A,BA,B be differential graded algebras and let PP be an AA-BB bimodule. The two actions commute with the differential. A vector in PP can therefore be acted on by AA from the left and by BB from the right, as an interface can be acted on from its two sides.

    The derived functors

    F=P⊗B𝐋−:D(B)⟶D(A),G=RHomA⁡(P,−):D(A)⟶D(B)F=P\otimes_B^{\mathbf L}-:D(B)\longrightarrow D(A), \qquad G=R\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,-):D(A)\longrightarrow D(B)
    (17.1)

    form an adjunction. Derived categories are used with their mapping complexes, as in Chapter 6. The right BB-action on PP produces the left BB-action on the Hom complex by precomposition. The actual unit and counit are

    ηL:L⟶GF(L),εM:FG(M)⟶M.\eta_L:L\longrightarrow GF(L), \qquad \varepsilon_M:FG(M)\longrightarrow M.
    (17.2)

    They compare the original object with the result of passing through the interface and back. If all units are equivalences, FF is fully faithful. The counit then identifies which objects of D(A)D(A) it reconstructs. Full faithfulness is already a reconstruction theorem on the image; equivalence with the whole target category requires that image to be the whole category.

    For a complete finite example, take A=Mn(k)A=M_n(k), B=kB=k, P=knP=k^n, and let EijE_{ij} be the matrix units. Put e=E11e=E_{11}. Then G(M)=eMG(M)=eM, and the counit is

    εM:kn⊗eM⟶M,vi⊗m⟼Ei1m.\varepsilon_M:k^n\otimes eM\longrightarrow M, \qquad v_i\otimes m\longmapsto E_{i1}m.
    (17.3)

    Its inverse is

    M⟶kn⊗eM,m⟼∑ivi⊗E1im.M\longrightarrow k^n\otimes eM, \qquad m\longmapsto\sum_i v_i\otimes E_{1i}m.

    The two composites are identities because E1jEi1=δijeE_{1j}E_{i1}=\delta_{ij}e and ∑iEi1E1i=1A\sum_iE_{i1}E_{1i}=1_A. The unit sends a vector vv to v1⊗vv_1\otimes v in e(kn⊗V)e(k^n\otimes V), so it is also an isomorphism. This proves the equivalence of module categories directly, including its maps.

    The same example shows why a centre alone is insufficient. The algebra of upper triangular two-by-two matrices over kk has centre kk, just as M2(k)M_2(k) does. It has two nonisomorphic simple modules, obtained by evaluating the two diagonal entries; M2(k)M_2(k) has one simple module up to isomorphism. Their module categories are not equivalent. A centre comparison and an interface equivalence answer different questions.

    In a field theory, PP is not an arbitrary bimodule selected to make (17.2) invertible. It must come from the prescribed line, junction or boundary condition. Its action, support and differential are part of the comparison. The finite matrix example gives the criterion to test; it does not identify any physical interface with knk^n.

    17.2 What the affine theorem reconstructs

    Take a simple complex Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak g, normalize its long roots to square length two, and write h∨h^\vee for its dual Coxeter number. Let s∈ℂ∖ℚs\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Q be the shifted level and B=Y−s(𝔤)B=Y_{-s}(\mathfrak g) the polynomial differential graded line algebra. The affine mode algebra AA has raw level s−h∨s-h^\vee. The module

    W=A⊗U(t𝔤[t])ℂW=A\otimes_{U(t\mathfrak g[t])}\mathbb C

    is generated by a vector annihilated by the positive currents, with the horizontal zero modes acting freely on its top. Its smooth right BB-action, homogeneous endomorphism comparison, coherent Taylor cutoffs on the Chevalley resolution, and enhanced tensor–Hom adjunction are the realization data of Chapter 6. Under these hypotheses the ordinary unit is invertible on every unbounded source complex. The resulting equivalence is

    D(B)≃Loc⁡(W).D(B)\simeq\operatorname{Loc}(W).
    (17.4)

    The right-hand category is generated inside the smooth affine target by WW under shifts, cones, coproducts and retracts, with all internal energy shifts in the energy-graded convention. The counit is the coreflection onto this category.

    Why can an unbounded conclusion follow from finite data? Write R=U(𝔤)R=U(\mathfrak g), let II be the positive-weight ideal in BB, and let DD be the number of positive roots of 𝔤\mathfrak g. The precise bimodule statement is

    I⊗R𝐋(D+1)≃0,I⊗R𝐋D≄0.I^{\otimes^{\mathbf L}_R(D+1)}\simeq0, \qquad I^{\otimes^{\mathbf L}_R D}\not\simeq0.
    (17.5)

    Each surviving positive factor raises energy and moves strictly up the finite Bruhat order in its integral linkage block. The length can rise at most DD times. A block in which all simple integral roots have positive mode realizes a longest word through actual embeddings of affine Verma modules, giving the nonzero power. For 𝔰𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_3, the three positive roots give a surviving cube and a vanishing fourth power. Equation (17.5) yields a tower with at most D+1D+1 coefficient layers inflated from RR. The original unit is already invertible on each such layer, so exact triangles give the conclusion on the source itself. The sharp exponent

    At a rational shifted level the zero-weight quotient can fail to detect the source. At raw 𝔰𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_2 level −3-3, a particular nonzero telescope vanishes on this quotient, has nonzero affine realization and has invertible original unit. Thus its affine image can retain precisely a source the quotient misses. At the critical raw level −h∨-h^\vee there are instead genuine nonzero realization kernels. The full rational classification and the relation between the cellular category and unbounded complexes with positive-current-torsion cohomology require additional arguments. A physical boundary must also supply its own functor, right adjoint and products.

    17.3 Products must survive passage through the interface

    An equivalence of linear categories can forget the way systems combine. If 𝒞\mathcal C and 𝒟\mathcal D have specified tensor products, a monoidal comparison includes maps

    γL,M:F(L)⊗𝒟F(M)⟶F(L⊗𝒞M)\gamma_{L,M}:F(L)\otimes_{\mathcal D}F(M) \longrightarrow F(L\otimes_{\mathcal C}M)
    (17.6)

    and a unit comparison. Their associativity square compares the two maps obtained from three inputs, and the unit diagrams compare insertion of the tensor unit. A strong monoidal functor requires these maps to be equivalences. A braided comparison also includes the exchange square and its compatibility with the associator.

    For local fields, the two tensor products in (17.6) may depend on positions and expansions. Chapter 12 supplies a complete positive example in the spectral class: the form ρz\rho_z defines fields, their exchange, the cross-contracted tensor product, and a level-indexed coproduct preserving the fields. The field hexagon is an identity on a stated Laurent expansion space. This is substantially more information than an abstract coproduct on state vectors.

    Chapter 8 supplies another positive result. For nonrational 𝔰𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_2, under its realization and finite-descent hypotheses, every finite tuple of ordinary unbounded line modules has a comparison with the independently defined radial current complex. Scalar extension to the shape field FF occurs before completion to F((q))F((q)). Rational evaluation and its affine restriction preserve the outgoing action and all stated incoming actions. Composition of the original kernels along a finite tree agrees on this common radial domain.

    That conclusion does not define substitution on every separately completed intermediate tensor. The series

    ∑n≥0qnλ−n2\sum_{n\geq0}q^n\lambda^{-n^2}

    is a valid element of ℂ(λ)((q))\mathbb C(\lambda)((q)), whereas substituting λ=zq\lambda=zq produces outer orders n−n2n-n^2 with no lower bound. The proposed substituted series is outside the iterated Laurent space. A larger tensor comparison must impose and prove the support estimates that exclude this failure, or choose a different independently justified domain.

    Likewise, an integral collision fibre cannot be obtained by setting the discriminant to zero in a space where it has been inverted. The finite integral heads in Chapter 8 carry actual derived collision maps before localization. Comparing those maps with the radial theorem requires the finite-head and completion comparisons together. A common formal expression is not a common domain.

    Native fields on every algebraic input

    The native four-colour construction has a dg quantum vertex structure on every algebraic input through the coefficient ring

    R3=ℂ[ℏ]/(ℏ3).R_3=\mathbb C[\hbar]/(\hbar^3).

    Its state complex is M3=VKB(𝔤𝔩2)⊗R3F0M_3=V^{KB}(\mathfrak{gl}_2)\otimes_{R_3}F_0, with the trace-current and trace-ghost factors retained. At every numerical level KK, including 00 and −2-2, the field 𝕐−\mathbb Y_-, translation, vacuum and exchange give a dg quantum vertex superalgebra on all algebraic states. The locality exponent depends on the first two states and works for every final state. The opposite field 𝕐+\mathbb Y_+ is a weakly associative chain field, joined to 𝕐−\mathbb Y_- by the specified field homotopy. A separate full quantum vertex structure for the opposite exchange is not part of this conclusion. All-input field theorem.

    Passing to cohomology removes the exchange correction. The exchange has an algebraically finite Laurent homotopy

    [dM⊗,Λ(u)]=SM(u)−1.[d_M^{\otimes},\Lambda(u)]=S_M(u)-1.

    For cycle representatives of the first two inputs, a finite power of the separation, depending on those representatives, clears its poles. The difference of the two exchanged products then becomes a coefficientwise boundary for every final cycle. Consequently H∙(M3,dM)H^\bullet(M_3,d_M) carries an ordinary local vertex superalgebra, with R3R_3-bilinear fields and the original faithful central R3R_3-action. Both ordered fields induce that same operation. The argument needs no Künneth identification over R3R_3, and ordinary locality does not make the singular products zero. Cohomology fields.

    There is a separate computation of the states at each fixed K≠−2K\ne-2. An algebraic chain frame preserves the native minimal inclusion and identifies

    Write b=[ωℏ]b=[\omega_\hbar] and let LL denote the displayed trace factor.     17.4 A bulk action and a universal centre

    In the ordinary associative case, Hochschild cochains

    C∙(B,B)=RHomB⊗Bop⁡(B,B)C^\bullet(B,B)=R\operatorname{Hom}_{B\otimes B^{\mathrm{op}}}(B,B)

    act coherently on derived BB-modules. This suggests a place for bulk observables that act compatibly on all boundary systems. In chiral geometry, however, the appropriate action problem includes the configuration opens, the tensor products, the pointing and the collision homotopies. Its representing object need not be the Hochschild complex of a two-dimensional test algebra.

    Chapter 7 defines one such geometric problem exactly. A pointed factorizing coalgebra (F,u)(F,u) is tested against the Chevalley coalgebra CC of the two-idempotent algebra. The complete character and action spaces are 𝒳(F,u)\mathcal X(F,u) and 𝒜C(F,u)\mathcal A_C(F,u). Multiplication and vacuum evaluation give

    Θ:𝒳(F,u)⟶𝒜C(F,u),Ψ:𝒜C(F,u)⟶𝒳(F,u),ΨΘ≃1.\Theta:\mathcal X(F,u)\longrightarrow\mathcal A_C(F,u), \qquad \Psi:\mathcal A_C(F,u)\longrightarrow\mathcal X(F,u), \qquad \Psi\Theta\simeq1.
    (17.7)

    Recognition asks whether the other composite is homotopic to the identity with all the required compatibilities. This is proved for the full families stated in Chapter 7: arbitrary pointings on genuinely unital Chevalley coalgebras, their specified module extensions, and the nonunital families covered by the horizontal-representative or commutative-connection theorems. The three-block filling for arbitrary coassociative actors requires no cocommutativity. The separate old-base closed-corner comparison has its own coherent cocommutativity hypothesis and remains on the separated locus.

    A universal geometric centre would represent the action space for every admitted pointed actor. Even if such representability is established, a bulk reconstruction still needs a map from the independently defined bulk observables to that centre. It must identify the actual action, its product and its support. The ordinary exterior-source mapping-space theorem is another exact positive result; it does not define this geometric bulk map by changing the name of its target.

    There is also an accomplished classical geometric reconstruction. Chapter 13 constructs the complete ordinary coefficient-family system of a fixed unital chiral algebra, with arbitrary classical parameter schemes, compatible vacuum insertions and collision equivalences. Realizing the vacuum and applying the geometric residue construction returns the original chiral algebra. This theorem explains what additional geometric information makes reconstruction possible. Its ordinary tensors and fixed algebra are part of its scope; its conclusion does not assert a derived reconstruction of an interacting bulk theory.

    17.5 States and amplitudes impose another comparison

    Return to the Gaussian of Chapter 1. Normalization produces a linear functional ω\omega with ω(1)=1\omega(1)=1. The unnormalized functional has the form

    Z(O)=Z(1)ω(O).Z(O)=Z(1)\,\omega(O).
    (17.8)

    Knowing ω\omega leaves the factor Z(1)Z(1) undetermined. If that factor varies in a line rather than as a scalar, one must also identify the line and its connection. This distinction survives when the finite integral becomes a field theory.

    Chapter 11 constructs a numerical normalized Gaussian on the original continued source graph. Its domain includes the fixed metric and density, 0<|q|<10<|q|<1, κ≠0\kappa\ne0, ℏ>0\hbar>0, a smooth integrable source in the stated small inverse neighbourhood, zero normal trace, and a supplied smooth Ward filling TμT_\mu. The even finite-cycle fields converge to a Radon Gaussian; the complete odd and mixed moments are given by the graded Wick rule. Odd variables are not assigned an ordinary probability law.

    The original weighted coefficient heat construction gives another object: a based local vacuum line with a nonzero finite-part section. It uses its own reflected realization, spectral gap, smooth source bounds and finite action integrals. In a finite spectral frame, the counterterm is added to the covariant connection because the response one-form enters that connection with a minus sign. This line result determines more than the normalized state. It does not claim a convergent bare infinite determinant product or a global holonomy theorem.

    A cap is a chosen filling of a boundary together with fields, boundary conditions and normalization that prepare a vector or functional in the specified boundary state space. If an anomaly makes the amplitude line-valued, that line belongs to the data. For a bulk observable OO, an exact cap comparison would take the form

    ZMbulk(O)=ZM∂(rM(O)),Z_M^{\mathrm{bulk}}(O) =Z_M^{\partial}\bigl(r_M(O)\bigr),
    (17.9)

    where rMr_M is the actual observable comparison and both sides take values in an identified amplitude line. This equation is a target, not a definition of ZM∂Z_M^{\partial} by the left-hand side. The state prepared by the filling must be constructed independently, and the comparison must commute with cutting and gluing.

    There is a Gaussian example for which one can follow an operation from the action all the way to an independently specified filling. Fix numerical ℏ,κ≠0\hbar,\kappa\ne0 and k=ℏκk=\hbar\kappa on the marked half-space with oriented transverse coordinate tt and tangential complex coordinate zz. In the mixed presentation the tests are partial forms in dt,dz‾dt,d\bar z, in two fields Φ,η\Phi,\eta. In abelian Chern–Simons theory they are full spatial forms. Every spatial form splits uniquely into a partial form and dzdz times a partial form. If ss denotes the suspension of the linear tests, the comparison is

    s(αeΦ)⟼−κ−1dz∧α,s(βeη)⟼(−1)deg⁡β+1β.s(\alpha e_\Phi)\longmapsto-\kappa^{-1}dz\wedge\alpha,\qquad s(\beta e_\eta)\longmapsto(-1)^{\deg\beta+1}\beta .

    The mixed boundary condition kills the tangential trace of β\beta, precisely the condition that the spatial form restrict to a multiple of dzdz. The change of variables identifies the unary differentials. On a mixed Wick contraction the factor kκ−1=ℏk\kappa^{-1}=\hbar gives the correct quantum coefficient with the signs from the displayed map. Thus the two complexes of regular compact kernels agree at every fixed field number, with disjoint products and the empty unit. On a proper oriented graph ray the one-form tested by the Wilson source is η−κ−1Φdz\eta-\kappa^{-1}\Phi\,dz. The second term contributes when the ray moves tangentially. The ray comparison transports the specified Cauchy propagator, framing and outgoing subtraction with these tests. The marked Gaussian change of variables

    At level one the neutral pair (a,−a)(a,-a) at (r,0)(r,0), with real aa and 0<r<10<r<1, gives a regulator factor r−a2r^{-a^2} times a coherent oscillator state. Independently coupling the harmonic disk to the real source 2aRe⁡h(r)2a\operatorname{Re}h(r) gives a Gaussian law in which mode nn has mean arnar^n and variance nn. After the Gaussian–Fock identification, the squared modulus of the ray wavefunction divided by its squared norm gives this same law. Acting on the wavefunction with the disk collar gives the same one-sided pairing. A different experiment uses positive-height cochain insertions, boundary creation modes and the two polynomial states (p12±p2)/2(p_1^2\pm p_2)/2. Their one-mode distributions agree, but the mixed observable in Chapter 11 has expectations +2+2 and −2-2. This is an actual discriminator on the common preparation domain.

    For numerical gravity the zero-height finite-stage Ward calculation and the full-source heat identities give specific operations on their own common domain. They retain the first quantum transport W0+χW1W^0+\chi W^1, χ=−ℏ\chi=-\hbar. To reach (17.9) one needs a physical cut, its quartet of fields, a compatible phase and an independently fixed filling. A useful conditional uniqueness statement follows from Wick recursion. Two normalized centered continuous Gaussian functionals with the same covariance and the same graded Wick recursion agree on polynomial tests by degree induction. Density in the common completed test space extends this equality. A shared nonzero base amplitude in the identified line then gives equality of the unnormalized functionals. The physical question includes establishing that recursion for the independently prepared cap and checking it across spatial sewing.

    17.6 Independent realizations test what reconstruction preserves

    The geometric and arithmetic families provide decisive tests of the same distinctions. In the M2 junction of Chapter 14, the group Tor1⁡\operatorname{Tor}_1, in cohomological degree −1-1, vanishes, but a flux cap from Tor2⁡\operatorname{Tor}_2, in cohomological degree −2-2, survives at every positive rank and nonzero numerical ℏ\hbar. Ordinary tensor composition gives the expected quotient, while the derived interface retains an additional bimodule. A reconstruction preserving only ordinary products would miss the flux operation.

    For compact states, Chapter 15 constructs relative Donaldson–Thomas operators before taking their traces. Their closure gives the inverse-Igusa series with its fixed normalization. The full three-boundary operation contains information that these traces omit: an explicit nonzero cyclic Hochschild class changes the state product while leaving the fibre-marked operation and every stated multiplication trace unchanged. Thus a numerical identity can be an exact theorem without characterizing the state algebra that produces it.

    Arithmetic gives a related example with a different meaning. The integer-summation and theta constructions retain the full multiplicities and produce the complete Weil trace. A positive representation of the critical part is also constructed. Its missing trace is exactly the contribution of nonreal centred zeros. The full positivity problem remains stronger than continuous duality or the existence of a cyclic vector. Integral normal operations further distinguish arithmetic tubes from their scalar points.

    An attaching map makes the remaining choices concrete. If j:U↪Xj:U\hookrightarrow X is the complement of a closed point ii, fix a coefficient LL on UU and a complex VV on the point. A map V→i∗Rj∗LV\to i^*Rj_*L specifies how the value on the point sees the punctured neighbourhood. The corresponding constructible sheaf is the homotopy pullback

    Rj∗L×i∗i∗Rj∗Lhi∗V.Rj_*L\mathop{\times}^{h}_{i_*i^*Rj_*L} i_*V .

    Restriction to UU recovers LL, and restriction to the point recovers VV. Restricting the projection from the glued sheaf to Rj∗LRj_*L gives the chosen arrow from VV to the link. For the four charge-one rays at level two, different lines in the two-dimensional degree-two cohomology of the deepest link, H2(i∗Rj∗L)H^2(i^*Rj_*L), give genuinely different perverse extensions with identical stalk and costalk dimensions. For identical rays, fix the coordinate framings and specify the positive half-exchange as +i+i. With that linearization the permutation action on H2(i∗Rj∗L)H^2(i^*Rj_*L) splits as the trivial character plus the sign character. Exactly their two lines in the projective family admit this equivariance. If the coefficient is further required to be the ordinary inverse image of a sheaf on the coarse unordered space, every stabilizer must act trivially on each stalk. This singles out the quotient by the trivial line, the pullback of the downstairs middle extension. The physical theory would have to supply that last requirement or decide between the two equivariant candidates in another way. The four-point attachment

    There are therefore several genuinely different ways to seek a common theory. One can try to characterize the bulk by its supported operations on every boundary object, reconstruct a collision algebra by attaching its coefficients, or characterize a state by measurements and a compatible filling. Each approach predicts something its input has left out. Agreement would require an interface that transports the actual attaching maps to the supported operations, composes them on the independent intermediate domains and carries the prescribed state through sewing. The next chapter gives examples small enough to tell these proposed reconstructions apart.

The outstanding comparisons have explicit tests, from a marked collision and a second sewing to a compact three-point measurement or a signed arithmetic trace.

    Part V Reconstruction and open problemsChapter 18 of 18

    18

    The strongest remaining questions

    There are three ways to ask how much of the bulk survives on a boundary. Insert a bulk field above the boundary and record its action on every boundary system. Follow a line as its endpoint collides with another endpoint and determine how the separated coefficient attaches to the collision. Or sew a filling to the boundary and measure the state it prepares. An equivalence of these descriptions would make a prediction. It would recover an attaching map or a sewing measurement which had not been used to define the comparison.

    The experiments in Chapters 4, 11 and 15 show exactly what this costs. For four charged lines at labelled positions, the full turns and a table of local dimensions permit a projective line of four-point attachments. With the specified half-exchange, permutation equivariance leaves two. Ordinary descent to the coarse quotient selects one. Whether the physical collision descends in this sense is an independent question. Two disk preparations can agree on each individual mode while a mixed insertion separates them. The trace and fibre-marked tube of a compact K3 state coefficient leave 1,750 independent first-order cubic directions invisible. In these cases more precise measurements can be named. A covariant map to the deepest link could choose an extension, a two-mode observable fixes a relative phase in the given pair, and a sharply sized family of cubic evaluations recovers the specified finite ambiguity.

    What makes the general problem difficult is composition. A measurement may determine a vector on one disk but give no continuation through the next sewing. A marked coefficient can have an algebraic comparison in all degrees while the independently constructed physical products have yet to realize either ordering. For that reason the central tests below use two independently chosen inputs, retain their original intermediate space, and compare an output that has mathematical meaning on both sides.
